name: Boniface felling the Donar Oak at Fritzlar
scope: T1: BONIFACE, an English monk born Winfrid in Devon, crosses the Rhine into the pagan lands of the Franks and Hessians in the 8th century to preach, sent with a commission from Pope Gregory II. T2: at FRITZLAR in Hesse in the year 723 he confronts the great oak sacred to DONAR (the German Thor), a tree the pagans hold inviolable, and takes up an AXE against it while a crowd of Franks stands watching, expecting the thunder-god to strike him dead. T3: after only a few blows a mighty WIND rises and the huge oak splits into FOUR PARTS and crashes to the ground; Donar sends no lightning; the pagans are astonished and many convert on the spot (this account is from Willibald's Vita Bonifatii, chapter 6, written c. 760). T4: from the wood of the fallen tree Boniface builds a CHAPEL dedicated to Saint Peter on the spot, turning the pagan cult-site into a Christian shrine — a template repeated across the mission. T5: decades later, on the fifth of June 754, at DOKKUM in Frisia while awaiting new converts for confirmation, Boniface is set upon by an armed band of pagans; he holds up a GOSPEL BOOK to shield his head, and a sword-blow cuts through the book and kills him; the RAGYNDRUDIS CODEX, still preserved at Fulda, is traditionally identified as that book, and its pages still bear the sword-gashes. Further rungs: Boniface's earlier crowning of Pepin the Short as king of the Franks; his correspondence with popes Gregory II, Gregory III, and Zachary; the archbishopric of Mainz; the modern legend that the Christmas tree originates from a fir Boniface pointed to standing near the felled oak (this fir tale is 19th-century folklore, not in Willibald).
source: Grokipedia 'Boniface' (browser); Willibald of Mainz, Vita Sancti Bonifatii, ch. 6 (Donar Oak) and ch. 8 (Dokkum martyrdom), c. 760; Wikipedia 'Saint Boniface' and 'Donar's Oak' for the Ragyndrudis Codex; primary: the Codex at Fulda.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T5 — the GOSPEL BOOK held up as a shield, cut through by the sword-blow, still preserved with the gashes visible at Fulda. Parents may know Boniface's name; almost none know the codex survives. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T2 swap Fritzlar for Geismar (which some sources use — actually the SAME event, but call it Fritzlar as most Grokipedia does; note the Geismar/Fritzlar naming as a real historical detail); at T3 swap 'four parts' for three / seven / twelve; at T4 swap Saint Peter for Saint Michael / Saint Martin / Saint Paul; at T5 swap the codex-name for other real Fulda relics. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T3 stem — 'Boniface swung his axe against the oak of Donar; a wind rose and the tree split into how many parts as it crashed down?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Thor's own axe-work in Norse myth — a cult-site desacralized by a numinous act. Plain 'Boniface' not 'the holy apostle to the Germans'. Distinguish HONESTLY: the axe-and-oak scene is Willibald's 8th-c. Vita — early hagiography, but WITHIN a generation of the man; the fir-tree-to-Christmas-tree tale is 19th-c. folklore, marked in Further rungs.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Carolingian expansion and Boniface's political role crowning Pepin. GEOGRAPHY owns Fritzlar as a place in Hesse. Theology owns the tree-felling STORY and the Ragyndrudis codex-as-shield story.

name: Wilfrid and the Synod of Whitby: the dating of Easter
scope: T1: in the 7th-century kingdom of Northumbria the Christian church is split between two customs — the CELTIC (Irish) tradition brought from IONA by monks like Aidan and Colman, and the ROMAN tradition brought by Augustine's mission from the south. T2: the split is most visible in the dating of EASTER: King OSWIU of Northumbria keeps the Celtic Easter while his queen EANFLED keeps the Roman date, so in some years the king is feasting Easter while the queen is still fasting Lent (Bede, Historia Ecclesiastica III.25). T3: in 664 Oswiu calls the SYNOD OF WHITBY at the double monastery of the abbess HILDA on the North Sea cliffs; COLMAN speaks for the Celtic side, citing the tradition of Saint COLUMBA and John the Evangelist; WILFRID, a young priest trained at Rome, speaks for the Roman side. T4: Wilfrid argues that the customs of Iona are those of a remote island against the practice of the whole Christian world — Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem — and cites PETER's authority as the keeper of the KEYS OF HEAVEN (Matthew 16:19); Oswiu asks Colman whether Peter truly received the keys, and Colman must agree. T5: Oswiu decides for ROME — 'I will not go against him, lest when I come to the gates of heaven there be no one to open them for me' (Bede, HE III.25); Colman and his Irish monks withdraw from Lindisfarne back to Iona rather than accept the change; Wilfrid becomes bishop of York. Further rungs: Hilda hosting the synod though she personally favors the Celtic side; Bede's dating of Easter method, the COMPUTUS, filling several chapters of his own works; Wilfrid's later stormy career including two banishments and appeals to Rome; the tonsure question (Celtic ear-to-ear vs. Roman crown) settled at the same synod.
source: Grokipedia 'Synod of Whitby' + 'Wilfrid' (browser); Bede, Historia Ecclesiastica Gentis Anglorum, Book III chapter 25 (the synod debate) and III.26 (Colman's withdrawal), completed 731; Wikipedia 'Synod of Whitby' for the modern reception; primary: Bede HE III.25.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T2 — the KING AND QUEEN keeping different Easters in the same palace, one feasting while the other fasts. That marital-liturgical mismatch stuns. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Iona for Lindisfarne (Lindisfarne is real, and Celtic-tradition, but the ORIGIN monastery is Iona — a genuine mine); at T3 swap Colman for Aidan (real predecessor, dead by 664) / Cedd (real translator at the synod); at T4 swap Matthew 16:19 for a wrong scripture; at T5 swap Iona for Kells / Skellig Michael. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T2 stem — 'In Northumbria's royal household the king kept one Easter date and the queen another. What was the DIFFERENCE this produced in a single palace across the same weeks?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell a legal dispute at a Norse thing or a Gaelic brehon judgment — a formal debate at a named place, decided by an agreed authority. This ladder specifically honors the coverage note about the WHITBY DATING BEING DOCUMENTED HISTORY (Bede within 70 years, using both sides' testimony) — treated as history-in-the-church, not as miracle.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the political consolidation of Northumbria and the Christianization of England. Theology owns the SYNOD-STORY and its decision. GEOGRAPHY owns Whitby cliffs and Lindisfarne as places.

name: Bede the Venerable at Jarrow: the church history of the English people
scope: T1: BEDE is given to the double monastery of MONKWEARMOUTH-JARROW in Northumbria at the age of SEVEN and remains there the rest of his life; he never travels farther than a few days' walk from the cloister but reads and writes his way through the entire learning of his day. T2: in 731, at about the age of 59, he finishes the HISTORIA ECCLESIASTICA GENTIS ANGLORUM ('The Ecclesiastical History of the English People'), in five books, dedicated to King CEOLWULF of Northumbria — the single most important source for early English Christian history. T3: the book tells stories other writers would have lost: the poet CAEDMON, the illiterate cowherd who dreams of a stranger commanding him to sing and wakes with the gift of English religious verse (HE IV.24); the SYNOD OF WHITBY and its Easter debate (HE III.25); Pope Gregory in the Roman slave-market seeing fair-haired English boys and saying 'Non Angli, sed angeli' ('not Angles, but angels') — Bede reports the pun and the mission it inspired (HE II.1). T4: Bede is called VENERABILIS ('the Venerable') in tradition (his relics at Durham read 'Hac sunt in fossa Bedae venerabilis ossa' — 'here in this grave are the bones of the venerable Bede'); he introduces the ANNO DOMINI dating system into general use in his Ecclesiastical History, cementing the way Western Europe will number its years. T5: on the eve of Ascension Day 735, dying at Jarrow, Bede is finishing his English TRANSLATION of the GOSPEL OF JOHN; his student CUTHBERT (later abbot) writes an EPISTOLA DE OBITU BEDAE describing the last day: Bede dictates all morning, then all afternoon; the boy scribe Wilberht says at evening, 'There is still one sentence, dear master, that we have not yet written down' — Bede answers 'WRITE IT QUICKLY'; the boy says 'It is finished now'; Bede says 'Thou hast well said. It is finished' and dies sitting on the floor of his cell singing 'Gloria Patri' (Cuthbert's letter, c. 735). Further rungs: Bede's Latin as a model for medieval historians; his hagiography of Cuthbert of Lindisfarne in both verse and prose; the OSWALD miracles Bede records; his DE TEMPORUM RATIONE calculating the age of the world.
source: Grokipedia 'Bede' (browser); Bede, Historia Ecclesiastica Gentis Anglorum, esp. II.1 (Angli/angeli), III.25 (Whitby), IV.24 (Caedmon); Cuthbert of Jarrow, Epistola de Obitu Bedae, c. 735; Wikipedia 'Bede'; primary: HE II.1, IV.24; the Cuthbert death-letter.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T5 — the LAST SENTENCE of the Gospel of John dictated as Bede is dying, and his 'IT IS FINISHED' echoing the words on the cross (Cuthbert's letter records both the sentence and the response). Parents know Bede's name; almost none know the death-scene detail. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Jarrow for Lindisfarne (real, adjacent — Cuthbert's monastery, not Bede's) / Iona (real, Columba's) / Whitby (real, Hilda's); at T3 swap 'Non Angli, sed angeli' attribution from Gregory to Augustine of Canterbury (real, later mission-leader, wrong attribution); at T4 swap Anno Domini for Dionysius Exiguus (real inventor; Bede POPULARIZED) — trap for over-eager students; at T5 swap the Gospel translated (John is right; Matthew / Mark / Luke are traps). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T5 stem — 'On Ascension eve Bede was dying but still dictating a translation. The boy said one sentence was left; Bede answered how?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Snorri Sturluson at Reykholt finishing the Prose Edda — a scholar in a specific cell writing what would define a civilization's memory of itself. 'Venerable' as tradition-earned title, not sanctity claim.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Anglo-Saxon Northumbria's political history. Theology owns Bede as the STORY-KEEPER of English Christianity and the Caedmon / Gregory / Whitby narratives he preserved. GEOGRAPHY owns Jarrow as a place.

name: Charlemagne and Alcuin at Aachen: the Palace School
scope: T1: CHARLEMAGNE, king of the Franks and later crowned emperor by Pope Leo III at Rome on Christmas Day 800, makes his capital at AACHEN (Aix-la-Chapelle) in what is now western Germany and builds there a stone PALATINE CHAPEL modeled on San Vitale at Ravenna — the oldest surviving stone church north of the Alps in its region. T2: Charlemagne meets the English deacon ALCUIN OF YORK — the finest scholar of the age, trained at York's cathedral library — in Italy at Parma in 781 and invites him north to head the PALACE SCHOOL at Aachen; Alcuin arrives with a nickname for himself, ALBINUS, and joins a court that also names Charlemagne DAVID and takes classical / biblical noms de plume for its scholars. T3: Alcuin's school teaches the SEVEN LIBERAL ARTS — trivium (grammar, rhetoric, dialectic) and quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy) — reviving Latin learning that had faded in the wake of the Western Empire's collapse; he supervises a great scriptorium producing corrected copies of the VULGATE Bible. T4: from this Aachen scholarship comes the CAROLINGIAN MINUSCULE — a clear rounded lowercase letterform, with word-spaces and simple punctuation, designed for legibility; it becomes the ancestor of modern printed Roman type (when Renaissance humanists later thought they were reviving Roman letters, they were actually reviving Carolingian minuscule). T5: the movement is called the CAROLINGIAN RENAISSANCE; when Charlemagne dies in 814 he is buried inside the Palatine Chapel at Aachen, seated on a MARBLE THRONE (still there — thirty-one German kings and emperors will later be crowned on it, from Otto I in 936 to Ferdinand I in 1531); Alcuin has retired before this to be abbot of Saint MARTIN of TOURS, dying in 804. Further rungs: Alcuin's letters — over 300 survive — including the earliest recorded phrase 'vox populi, vox Dei' (which he attacks, not endorses, in a letter to Charlemagne c. 798); the young ANGILBERT and EINHARD as pupils; Einhard's later Vita Karoli Magni giving us Charlemagne's physical description (tall, thick neck, love of swimming); the tale that Charlemagne, though a mighty king, could BARELY WRITE his own name and kept tablets under his pillow to practice (Einhard, Vita Karoli 25).
source: Grokipedia 'Charlemagne' + 'Alcuin' + 'Carolingian Renaissance' (browser); Einhard, Vita Karoli Magni, esp. chapters 25 and 31, c. 830; Wikipedia 'Palatine Chapel, Aachen' and 'Carolingian minuscule'; primary: Einhard chapters cited.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T4 — the LETTERS YOU ARE READING RIGHT NOW are descended from Carolingian minuscule via the Renaissance humanists who mistook it for Roman. That connection stuns modern readers. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Aachen for Paris (the Frankish court was NOT yet at Paris — a real trap) / Rome / Reims; at T2 swap Alcuin's origin from York (right) to Canterbury / Iona / Wearmouth; at T4 swap Carolingian minuscule for uncial (real earlier script) / Gothic blackletter (real later script); at T5 swap 'thirty-one' kings crowned on the marble throne for other real numbers. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T4 stem — 'The lowercase letters used across modern Latin-alphabet Europe descend, through Renaissance revival, from a script designed at Charlemagne's court. What is that script called?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell the Athenian gathering of philosophers under Pericles or the Njal-saga law-council — a court that made a civilization by naming its rules. Charlemagne's near-illiteracy is a real Einhard detail — kept in.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Charlemagne as first Holy Roman Emperor and the political consolidation of the Franks. Theology owns Alcuin at the Palace School and the Vulgate revision as STORY of Christian learning revived. GEOGRAPHY owns Aachen as a place.

name: Cyril and Methodius: the Slavic alphabet
scope: T1: two Greek brothers from THESSALONICA — CONSTANTINE (who takes the monastic name CYRIL) and METHODIUS — grow up in a city where the Slavic language is widely heard; the elder is a monk-administrator, the younger a philosopher-linguist teaching at Constantinople. T2: in 862 Prince RASTISLAV of GREAT MORAVIA (a Slavic principality centered in what is now the Czech Republic / Slovakia) sends to the Byzantine emperor Michael III asking for missionaries who can preach in the Slavic tongue rather than in Latin or Greek; the emperor sends the two brothers. T3: on the way, Cyril designs a new ALPHABET to render the sounds of Slavic — historians call his original design GLAGOLITIC (from the Slavic 'glagol', 'word'); a later simplified script derived from it and named for him is called CYRILLIC (developed by his students after his death, using Greek majuscules for most letters), and it is the ancestor of the alphabets still used across Russia, Ukraine, Bulgaria, Serbia and beyond. T4: they translate the GOSPELS and the liturgy into OLD CHURCH SLAVONIC, and Cyril defends the use of Slavic in worship at a debate in VENICE in 867 against the 'trilinguists' who insisted worship could only be in Hebrew, Greek, or Latin — the languages Pilate had written above the cross (John 19:20); Cyril answers, 'Does not God's rain fall equally on all, and does not the sun shine equally on all?' T5: they carry the RELICS of Pope CLEMENT I, found by Cyril in Crimea (bones tied to an anchor cast into the sea), as a gift to Pope Adrian II in Rome; the pope receives the relics AND blesses the Slavic liturgy on the altar of Santa Maria Maggiore in 868. Cyril dies in Rome February 14, 869, and is buried at San Clemente there — his tomb visible in the lower church today; Methodius goes back north as archbishop, dies at Velehrad in 885, and the mission is expelled from Moravia but survives in Bulgaria under Boris I, from where the Cyrillic script and Slavic liturgy spread east to Kievan Rus. Further rungs: the KHAZAR mission earlier in Cyril's career; the argument at Venice quoted in the Vita Constantini; the two brothers named CO-PATRONS OF EUROPE by Pope John Paul II in 1980; the ORTHODOX churches celebrate them May 11.
source: Grokipedia 'Cyril and Methodius' + 'Glagolitic script' + 'Cyrillic script' (browser); Vita Constantini (9th-c. Old Church Slavonic hagiography); Wikipedia 'Saints Cyril and Methodius'; primary: Vita Constantini for the Venice debate quote.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T3 — the SCRIPT DIFFERENCE — Cyril's own invention was GLAGOLITIC (blocky, strange-looking); the CYRILLIC named for him was developed by his STUDENTS after his death. Almost no one knows this. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Thessalonica for Constantinople (real, but their WORKPLACE, not birthplace); at T2 swap Rastislav's Moravia for Kievan Rus (real, later Slavic Christianization, wrong century); at T3 swap Glagolitic and Cyrillic (invite the mine); at T4 swap the trilinguist languages (Latin / Greek / Hebrew are right; Latin / Greek / Aramaic is the trap — the Pilate inscription is the source and it's Hebrew there); at T5 swap San Clemente for Santa Maria Maggiore (both real, both in the story — Cyril's TOMB is San Clemente). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T3 stem — 'Cyril designed a new alphabet to write the sounds of the Slavic language. Historians call his original design not Cyrillic but ______ (from the Slavic word for word).' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Ulfilas designing the Gothic alphabet to translate scripture for the Goths — a linguist-missionary answering a specific need at a named court. No 'Apostles to the Slavs' triumphal frame; the honest details are more remarkable than any epithet.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns 9th-c. Moravian and Byzantine politics. Theology owns the alphabet-creation and the Venice trilinguist debate STORIES. GEOGRAPHY owns the modern Cyrillic-alphabet countries as places.

name: Cuthbert of Lindisfarne and the otters warming his feet
scope: T1: CUTHBERT enters the monastery of MELROSE on the Scottish borders as a boy after a vision the night the Irish missionary Aidan died; he becomes a monk under the abbot EATA, trained in the Celtic tradition. T2: he moves later to LINDISFARNE — the tidal 'Holy Island' off the Northumbrian coast, cut off from the mainland twice a day by the incoming sea — and becomes its prior; he preaches through remote hill villages that had lapsed into paganism, walking sometimes weeks at a time to reach one settlement. T3: seeking greater solitude he retreats to the tiny island of INNER FARNE, a rocky outcrop in the North Sea south of Lindisfarne; he builds a cell with walls high enough that he can only see the sky, digs a well in the rock, and lives on barley he grows himself. T4: Bede tells (Vita Sancti Cuthberti, chapter 10, c. 720) that one night a monk from Coldingham spied on Cuthbert secretly and saw him wading into the SEA up to his neck to spend the night singing psalms; when he came out at dawn two OTTERS ran up from the tide, warmed his feet with their breath, and dried them with their fur before returning to the water. T5: consecrated bishop of Lindisfarne against his will in 685, Cuthbert serves only two years before returning to Inner Farne to die; his body is buried at Lindisfarne, and eleven years later (698) the monks OPEN the coffin and find the body INCORRUPT — this becomes his most famous miracle. When Viking raids destroy Lindisfarne (the great raid of 793 is the first Viking attack on England), the monks carry his coffin across northern England for over a century until it comes to rest at DURHAM, where the cathedral is built over him and his tomb remains today; the LINDISFARNE GOSPELS, illuminated in his honor c. 700, survive in the British Library. Further rungs: the eider ducks of the Farne Islands still called CUTHBERT'S DUCKS (or 'cuddy ducks') because he protected them; Bede's two Vitae of Cuthbert (verse and prose); the Coldingham monk's secret watch as source for the otter story — Bede names the informant; the coffin at Durham opened again in 1104 and again in 1827, body found in fragments but with recognizable relics.
source: Grokipedia 'Cuthbert' (browser); Bede, Vita Sancti Cuthberti, esp. chapter 10 (sea and otters); Bede, HE IV.28 (Cuthbert's episcopate) and IV.30 (incorrupt body); Wikipedia 'Cuthbert' and 'Lindisfarne Gospels'; primary: Vita Sancti Cuthberti c. 10.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T4 — the OTTERS WARMING HIS FEET WITH THEIR BREATH after a night in the sea. This is Bede's actual text and it's unforgettable. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Melrose for Iona / Lindisfarne (Lindisfarne is his LATER house — real trap) / Whitby; at T3 swap Inner Farne for the Skellig Michael (real Irish hermit island, wrong figure); at T4 swap otters for seals (real Farne coast animal) / ravens / puffins; at T5 swap Durham for York (real Northumbrian see) / Lindisfarne (real, but the body MOVED). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T4 stem — 'A monk of Coldingham secretly watched Cuthbert one night. What did he see two sea creatures do at dawn?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Fionn's animal companions or Saint Kevin at Glendalough with the blackbird nesting in his palm — a hermit-saint's peaceable-kingdom moment. HONEST distinction (per coverage note): the OTTERS story is Bede's hagiography — 8th-c., pious tradition, marked HERE as 'Bede tells' rather than as history. The INCORRUPT BODY finding and the Durham translation are documented monastic events, though the interpretation is faith.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Viking raids on Lindisfarne 793. GEOGRAPHY owns Lindisfarne, Inner Farne, and Durham cathedral. Theology owns the otters story and the incorrupt body and translation traditions.

name: Thomas Becket at Canterbury: 'four knights and a broken sword-tip'
scope: T1: THOMAS BECKET is chancellor to King HENRY II of England — the two men close friends, hunting and drinking together — until Henry has him made ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY in 1162, believing his friend will help him control the church. T2: Becket surprises the king by turning strict churchman, resisting royal jurisdiction over 'criminous clerks' (clergy accused of secular crimes) and the CONSTITUTIONS OF CLARENDON that Henry issues in 1164 to limit church courts; the quarrel drives Becket into six years of exile in France. T3: after a fragile reconciliation Becket returns to England in December 1170 and immediately excommunicates the bishops who had crowned Henry's son without him. Henry, at his Christmas court in Normandy, hearing this, cries out in fury — the famous phrase preserved as 'WILL NO ONE RID ME OF THIS TURBULENT PRIEST?' (the exact wording is a later paraphrase; contemporary chroniclers give variants like 'What miserable drones and traitors have I nourished... that they let their lord be treated with such shameful contempt by a low-born clerk?'). T4: FOUR KNIGHTS — Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy, and Richard le Breton — take Henry at his word, cross the Channel, and confront Becket in CANTERBURY CATHEDRAL on the afternoon of December 29, 1170. Becket refuses to flee, meets them in the north transept as monks try to bar the door, and answers, 'FOR THE NAME OF JESUS AND THE PROTECTION OF THE CHURCH I AM READY TO EMBRACE DEATH' (Edward Grim, eyewitness account, c. 1180). T5: FitzUrse strikes first, then Tracy; the third blow shears off the CROWN of Becket's head; the fourth knight, Richard le Breton, drives so hard that his SWORD-TIP BREAKS on the PAVEMENT stones (Grim's account is explicit: 'the point of the sword was broken against the pavement'). A subdeacon named Hugh of Horsea then puts his foot on Becket's neck and scatters his brains onto the floor with the sword-tip, saying 'Let us away, knights — this fellow will arise no more.' Within three years the pope canonizes Becket; his shrine at Canterbury becomes the greatest pilgrimage site in England (destination of Chaucer's pilgrims); King Henry does public penance walking barefoot to the shrine and being scourged by the monks in 1174. Further rungs: Becket's HAIR SHIRT crawling with vermin, discovered under his archbishop's robes as monks prepared the body, causing gasps of shock (Grim); the shrine covered in gold and jewels, destroyed by Henry VIII in 1538; T.S. Eliot's 'Murder in the Cathedral' (1935); the four knights fleeing to Knaresborough and later going on penitential pilgrimage.
source: Grokipedia 'Thomas Becket' (browser); Edward Grim, Vita Sancti Thomae, c. 1180 (eyewitness — Grim was in the transept and had his arm hacked trying to shield Becket); William FitzStephen and John of Salisbury (both eyewitnesses); Wikipedia 'Assassination of Thomas Becket'; primary: Grim's Vita for the quotes and the broken sword-tip.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T5 — the SWORD-TIP BROKEN ON THE PAVEMENT (Grim's actual line) and the HAIR SHIRT crawling with vermin found under the robes. The broken sword-tip is one of the most specific eyewitness details in medieval hagiography. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T3 swap the famous line's WORDING — offer both the paraphrase 'turbulent priest' and the chronicler variants; the paraphrase is a later polish, not verbatim (an important honest distinction); at T4 swap the four knights' names (all real, all recorded — but easy to mix); at T5 swap the pavement-broken sword-tip for other combat details (crown of the head is right — Grim's word is 'coronam capitis'). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T5 stem — 'The fourth knight's blow drove so hard against Becket's fallen body that something SNAPPED against the stone pavement. What?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Cuchulainn's death tied to the standing-stone facing his enemies, or Roland breaking Durendal at Roncesvalles — a warrior-saint (in this case a churchman standing his ground) facing named killers with a named quote. Honest on the 'turbulent priest' PARAPHRASE vs. the actual variant chronicler wordings. Grim as eyewitness cited by NAME.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Henry II's Angevin empire and the church-state jurisdictional dispute. Theology owns the Becket martyrdom-STORY, the pilgrim-cult (Chaucer's frame), and the shrine-destruction under Henry VIII. GEOGRAPHY owns Canterbury Cathedral as a place.

name: Francis of Assisi stripping naked in the town square
scope: T1: FRANCIS is born Giovanni di Pietro di Bernardone in ASSISI c. 1181, son of the wealthy cloth-merchant Pietro Bernardone; his mother nicknames him FRANCESCO ('the little Frenchman') for her husband's love of French goods. T2: after riding to the war with Perugia as a young cavalier and being captured for a year, and after a long illness on his return, he begins to give away his father's cloth and money to rebuild the derelict chapel of SAN DAMIANO outside Assisi — obeying, he says, a crucifix that spoke to him there: 'Francis, go and repair my house, which as you see is falling into ruin' (Legenda Trium Sociorum). T3: his father Pietro, furious at the wasted merchandise, drags him before the BISHOP OF ASSISI, Guido, in the piazza in front of the cathedral, demanding restitution and disinheritance. T4: Francis strips off ALL HIS CLOTHES in the public square and lays them at his father's feet — even his undergarments — and hands over the purse of coins, saying, 'Until now I have called Pietro Bernardone my father; but from now on I can say only OUR FATHER WHO ART IN HEAVEN' (Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima, c. 1229). The bishop wraps his cloak around the naked young man. T5: from that day (c. 1206) Francis dresses in a rough tunic tied with a rope, calls himself 'the little poor man' — POVERELLO — and begins to preach to whoever will listen; a first companion, BERNARD OF QUINTAVALLE, sells all he has to join him, then Peter Catani and Giles; when there are twelve, Francis walks to ROME in 1210 and gains Pope Innocent III's provisional approval for a new order — the FRIARS MINOR ('lesser brothers'). Further rungs: the earlier scene of Francis meeting the LEPER on the road below Assisi, dismounting and embracing him and giving him money (Testament of Francis, 1226 — Francis names this as the turning point); the CROSS OF SAN DAMIANO speaking; Francis's father allegedly cursing him from a doorway every time he passed thereafter (Celano); the piazza scene painted by Giotto in the Upper Church at Assisi c. 1297-99.
source: Grokipedia 'Francis of Assisi' (browser); Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima Sancti Francisci, c. 1229 (the disinheritance and stripping); Legenda Trium Sociorum, c. 1246 (the San Damiano voice); Francis's own Testament, 1226 (the leper); Wikipedia 'Francis of Assisi'; primary: Celano Vita Prima ch. 15.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T4 — Francis handing back EVEN HIS UNDERGARMENTS in the public square, and saying 'now I can say ONLY OUR FATHER WHO ART IN HEAVEN'. The absoluteness of the renunciation, in public, in front of his father, at grade-10 level is startling. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Assisi for Perugia (adjacent, real war-enemy) / Rimini / Siena; at T2 swap San Damiano for the Portiuncula (real, Francis's OTHER restored chapel — a genuine mine); at T5 swap the FRIARS MINOR order name for the DOMINICANS (real, contemporary order, black-and-white habit — see next ladder) / the CARMELITES; swap Innocent III for Honorius III (real, later pope who confirmed the Rule). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T4 stem — 'In the piazza in front of the bishop, what did Francis do with his clothes, and what did he then say about calling any man father?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Diogenes tossing his last bowl seeing a boy drink from cupped hands, or a Norse warrior renouncing gold at a lawspeaker's feet — a public radical divestment. No sanctity gloss; the ACTION carries the meaning. Named eyewitness source (Celano) so kids can trace it.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns 13th-century Italian city-state economics and the papal politics of Innocent III. Theology owns the Franciscan-origin STORY. GEOGRAPHY owns Assisi as a place.

name: Francis: the wolf of Gubbio and the sermon to the birds
scope: T1: near the Umbrian hill-town of GUBBIO, some years after founding his order, Francis hears that a great WOLF has been killing not only sheep but also PEOPLE, so terrifying the townspeople they will not go outside the walls except in armed bands (Fioretti di San Francesco, chapter 21, c. 1390 — a later compilation). T2: Francis walks out alone to meet the wolf; when the wolf charges him with open jaws, Francis makes the sign of the cross and calls, 'Come here, BROTHER WOLF' — the wolf closes its mouth, lies down at his feet 'like a lamb'. T3: Francis rebukes the wolf for its killings but then proposes a PACT: if the wolf will stop killing, the townspeople of Gubbio will feed the wolf every day for the rest of its life; the wolf lifts its RIGHT PAW and places it in Francis's hand as a promise. T4: at ASSISI c. 1213, Francis is walking through the plain near Bevagna and sees a great multitude of BIRDS of many kinds — doves, crows, jackdaws — sitting in a field; he leaves his companions in the road and walks in among them, and they do not fly away; he preaches: 'MY LITTLE SISTERS the BIRDS, much are you beholden to God your creator, and always and in every place ought you to praise him' (Fioretti ch. 16); the birds bow their heads, spread their wings, open their beaks, and only fly away when he makes the sign of the cross over them and gives them leave. T5: Francis composes near the end of his life the CANTICLE OF THE SUN (or Canticle of the Creatures, c. 1224-25) — 'Laudato si', mi Signore, per frate Sole' — praising God through BROTHER SUN, SISTER MOON, brother wind, sister water, brother fire, sister our mother EARTH, and (added on his deathbed) SISTER BODILY DEATH from whom no living person can escape; this is the earliest surviving poem in the ITALIAN vernacular, sung at Francis's own request on the night he died. Further rungs: the Gubbio wolf lived two more years fed by the townspeople and was mourned when it died of old age (Fioretti); the historical distinction — the WOLF and BIRDS stories come from the Fioretti, a 14th-c. compilation of Franciscan legends, not from the earliest Vita by Celano; the Canticle of the Sun is unquestionably Francis's own text (surviving in his companions' testimony); Pope Francis (2013- ) took his name from Francis of Assisi and named his 2015 encyclical LAUDATO SI' after the Canticle's opening line.
source: Grokipedia 'Francis of Assisi' + 'Fioretti of Saint Francis' + 'Canticle of the Sun' (browser); Fioretti di San Francesco chapters 16 (birds) and 21 (Gubbio wolf), late 14th c.; the Canticle preserved in Francis's own words c. 1224-25; Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima; Wikipedia 'Wolf of Gubbio'; primary: Fioretti chapters 16, 21; the Canticle.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T3 — the WOLF LIFTING ITS PAW to seal the pact. Everyone remembers 'Francis preached to the animals' vaguely; almost none remember the specific gesture. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Gubbio for Assisi (his home town — a trap because kids think everything is Assisi) / Perugia / La Verna (real, but that's the stigmata mountain); at T4 swap the birds' location (Bevagna is right; Alverna / Assisi / Siena are traps); at T5 swap the Canticle's authorship — some students may know it as 'Francis's Prayer' — and confuse it with the LATER 'Peace Prayer of Saint Francis' which was actually written in France c. 1912 (an important honest distinction). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T3 stem — 'Francis and the wolf made a pact — the town would feed it, it would stop killing. How did the wolf SEAL the pact?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Cuchulainn's earlier bond with the hound of Culann or Fionn's dogs Bran and Sceolan hunting alongside — a hero speaking to animals as kin. Honest distinction: the Gubbio wolf is FIORETTI (14th-c. legend compilation), the Canticle is definitely Francis's own composition (1224).
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Gubbio and Assisi as places. Theology owns the wolf and birds stories AND the Canticle of the Sun as literary origin of the Italian vernacular.

name: Francis: the stigmata at La Verna and the creche at Greccio
scope: T1: on Christmas night 1223, at the hilltop village of GRECCIO in the Rieti valley, Francis stages the FIRST NATIVITY SCENE (Italian PRESEPIO) using a live OX and a live ASS by a manger of straw — not statues, not a play, but a tableau to help the villagers picture the poverty of Bethlehem (Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima ch. 30). Francis reads the Gospel and preaches; one witness later swore he saw the infant Jesus lying in the manger himself. T2: less than a year later, in August 1224, Francis withdraws for a forty-day fast to the remote mountain hermitage of LA VERNA in the Tuscan Apennines, given him years before by Count Orlando of Chiusi; he goes with only Brother Leo and a few companions. T3: on or about September 14 (Feast of the Exaltation of the Cross), praying at dawn on a cliff of La Verna, Francis sees a vision of a six-winged SERAPH — a burning angel with the form of the crucified Christ pinned within its wings; the vision comes toward him and pierces him. T4: when the vision leaves, marks appear on Francis's body: on his hands and feet, wounds like NAIL-HEADS with the flesh of iron-black protrusions bent over as if clinched on the underside; on his right side a lance-wound bleeding fresh blood — the STIGMATA, the first documented case in Christian history (Celano, Vita Prima ch. 94-95; Bonaventure, Legenda Maior ch. 13). T5: Francis lives two more years with the wounds, hiding them under his tunic and sleeves; his body's failure accelerates — he goes nearly blind, is cauterized on the temple with a red-hot iron for eye disease; on the evening of October 3, 1226, he asks to be laid naked on the bare ground of the Portiuncula chapel outside Assisi, has the Passion narrative from John's Gospel read aloud, and dies with the stigmata visible — his brothers weep and touch the wounds, and hundreds file past the body over the next hours. He is canonized less than two years later (1228) by Pope Gregory IX, who had known him personally. Further rungs: the specific description of the stigmata Celano gives — flesh formed into iron-nail heads with the point coming out the palm and bent over on the back — is unlike any later stigmatic; the Greccio creche as the origin of every modern Christmas nativity scene; Bonaventure's Legenda Maior (1263) becoming the official life; Francis and Clare receiving the tonsure together at the Portiuncula in 1212.
source: Grokipedia 'Francis of Assisi' + 'Stigmata' + 'Nativity scene' (browser); Thomas of Celano, Vita Prima Sancti Francisci, ch. 30 (Greccio) and ch. 94-95 (stigmata), c. 1229; Bonaventure, Legenda Maior, ch. 13, 1263; Wikipedia 'Greccio' and 'La Verna'; primary: Celano chapters cited.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T1 — the FIRST NATIVITY SCENE with a LIVE OX AND ASS staged by Francis at GRECCIO in 1223. Every modern creche descends from this. Parents don't know Francis invented it. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Greccio for Assisi / Bethlehem / Rome; at T2 swap La Verna for Mount Alverna spelling / Monte Cassino (real, Benedict's mountain) / Subiaco (real, Benedict's cave); at T4 swap the FIVE stigmata locations for other biblical wound-configurations; at T5 swap October 3 (Francis's transitus) for October 4 (his feast day — the calendar issue is real). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T1 stem — 'On Christmas night 1223, at a hilltop village called Greccio, Francis staged something for the first time using a live ox and a live ass and a manger of straw. What did he create?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Odin's self-wounding on Yggdrasil for wisdom (Havamal) — a body deliberately marked as a numinous encounter, described in specific physical detail. The stigmata is described with Celano's exact physical detail (nail-form flesh) — kids can handle this and should. HISTORICAL vs LEGEND: the stigmata is DOCUMENTED by eyewitnesses (Celano interviewed those who saw the body); the Greccio scene is documented by Celano within three years; the manger-witness seeing baby Jesus is one villager's later testimony.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns La Verna and Greccio as places. Theology owns the stigmata and creche stories.

name: Clare of Assisi running to Francis in the night
scope: T1: CHIARA OFFREDUCCIO — CLARE — is the daughter of a noble family of Assisi, twelve years younger than Francis; when Francis's preaching begins to draw crowds in the streets and squares she listens from her family's palazzo. T2: on the night of PALM SUNDAY, March 18-19, 1212, Clare — refusing an arranged noble marriage — slips out of her father's house by a hidden 'DOOR OF THE DEAD' (a small door usually opened only to carry a corpse out) and RUNS through the dark down the hill to the little chapel of the PORTIUNCULA where Francis and his brothers wait. T3: Francis meets her at the chapel door with a torch procession; he CUTS OFF her long HAIR, receives her vows, and clothes her in a rough tunic like his own; she is 18 years old. T4: Clare's family arrives at the convent of San Paolo where she has been placed for safety and tries to drag her home; she runs to the altar, throws back her veil to show her SHORN HEAD, and clings to the altar cloth — the family withdraws. Within days her younger sister AGNES joins her; when the men come for Agnes, tradition holds that Agnes's body becomes so HEAVY they cannot lift her (Legenda Sanctae Clarae Virginis, ch. 4, c. 1256). T5: Clare settles at SAN DAMIANO (the same chapel Francis had rebuilt with his stripped-off riches) and founds the ORDER OF POOR LADIES (later the POOR CLARES); she is abbess for forty-two years, most of them in ill health, never leaving the enclosure. In 1240 SARACEN mercenaries (Frederick II's troops) attack Assisi and reach the walls of San Damiano; too sick to stand, Clare has herself carried out into the courtyard holding a MONSTRANCE containing the consecrated host — the Saracens turn away without attacking. She dies at San Damiano on August 11, 1253, two days after Pope Innocent IV himself has visited her bedside and delivered the papal bull PRIVILEGE OF POVERTY confirming her rule; she is canonized in 1255. Further rungs: Clare's writings including four letters to Agnes of Prague — the earliest surviving letters by a woman-founder of a religious order; Clare's early biographer Thomas of Celano (also Francis's biographer); the modern patronage of Clare as PATRON OF TELEVISION (proclaimed by Pius XII in 1958) because of an incident when, too ill to attend Christmas Mass at the Portiuncula, she reported seeing and hearing it on the wall of her cell.
source: Grokipedia 'Clare of Assisi' (browser); Thomas of Celano, Legenda Sanctae Clarae Virginis, c. 1256; Wikipedia 'Clare of Assisi' and 'Poor Clares'; primary: Legenda Clarae ch. 4 (Agnes and the heavy body) and Clare's own letters to Agnes of Prague, 1234-1253.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T2 — the 'DOOR OF THE DEAD' as her escape door in the night. The Assisi palazzos actually had these small side-doors for carrying corpses out, and Clare used one at 18 to run to a chapel. Modern kids find this thrilling. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Clare's family status (noble is right; peasant is the misconception mine); at T3 swap the Portiuncula for San Damiano (San Damiano is her LATER house — a genuine mine); at T5 swap the monstrance-Saracen story location for other Assisi churches; swap Poor Clares' order-name for Franciscans / Benedictines. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T2 stem — 'On Palm Sunday night 1212, Clare slipped out of her father's palazzo by a small side-door normally opened only for one purpose. What was that door for?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Deirdre of the Sorrows fleeing to be with Naoise, or Brynhild in her wall of flame waiting for Sigurd — a young woman making an irrevocable choice against her family in the night. Clare's radicalism kept whole (not softened into 'Francis's follower'); she is her own founder.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns Assisi. Theology owns the escape-STORY, the Saracen-monstrance STORY, and the Poor Clares as story of women's religious life.

name: Dominic and the black-and-white habit
scope: T1: DOMINIC de Guzman is born c. 1170 in the Castilian village of CALERUEGA; his mother JANE OF AZA is a noblewoman later beatified in her own right; while pregnant with Dominic she dreams that a DOG runs out of her womb with a burning TORCH in its mouth and sets fire to the world (an image later punned on: 'Dominicanes' = Domini canes = 'the Lord's dogs'). T2: as a young canon at the cathedral of OSMA, Dominic travels in 1203 through southern France with his bishop Diego and sees the CATHARS (Albigensians) — a heretical dualist movement — deeply established because their traveling preachers WALK BAREFOOT while the Catholic legates ride with baggage-trains. Dominic determines that the church needs a preaching order that owns nothing. T3: in 1215 he gathers a small band of followers at TOULOUSE and, in 1216, receives papal approval from Honorius III for the ORDO PRAEDICATORUM ('Order of Preachers') — the DOMINICANS. Their habit is the WHITE TUNIC AND BLACK MANTLE that gives them their nickname 'Blackfriars'; white for purity, black for penance. T4: Dominic sends his handful of brothers OUT ACROSS EUROPE almost immediately — 'Hoarded seed does not bear fruit' (Jordan of Saxony, Libellus, c. 1233); within twelve months brothers are studying at PARIS and BOLOGNA (the two great universities of the age); the order becomes intellectually formidable, producing within thirty years its greatest star: THOMAS AQUINAS. T5: tradition (recorded in the 15th century by Blessed Alan de la Roche) attributes the ROSARY prayer to Dominic — a chain of beads for counting Ave Marias, given to him in a vision by the Virgin during his fight against the Cathars; modern historical scholarship dates the Marian-bead prayer to earlier monastic 150-Aves-for-the-illiterate customs. Dominic dies at Bologna on August 6, 1221; his last words to his brothers are, 'Have charity for one another; guard humility; make your treasure out of voluntary poverty' (Jordan of Saxony); he is buried in the church of San Domenico, Bologna, where his marble tomb-arca is carved by Nicola Pisano and (a century later) by the young MICHELANGELO, who at age 19 carves three of the small figures (St Petronius, St Proculus, and a candle-bearing angel — his earliest signed sculpture in Bologna, 1494). Further rungs: Dominic's contemporary FRANCIS OF ASSISI met him in Rome in 1215; the two founder-orders (Dominicans / Franciscans) as parallel innovations; the DOMINICAN role in the Inquisition (from 1233) as honest historical complication; the ROSARY's actual medieval development traced to Prussian monasticism.
source: Grokipedia 'Dominic' + 'Dominican Order' + 'Rosary' (browser); Jordan of Saxony, Libellus de principiis Ordinis Praedicatorum, c. 1233; Wikipedia 'Saint Dominic' and 'Rosary'; primary: Jordan of Saxony's Libellus.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T5 — MICHELANGELO at 19 carving three figures on Dominic's tomb-arca in Bologna in 1494 — his first signed sculpture. That connection between Dominic and Michelangelo is astonishing and true. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Caleruega (Spain, right) for a French / Italian birthplace (Dominic is often assumed Italian because of the Bologna death — a real mine); at T2 swap Cathars for Waldensians (real, contemporary movement) / Bogomils (real, further east); at T3 swap the habit-colors (white tunic, black mantle is right; brown-and-white is Carmelite, all-brown is Franciscan, all-white is Cistercian); at T5 swap the ROSARY-tradition attribution — flag the historical distinction. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T3 stem — 'The Dominicans are also called BLACKFRIARS because of the color of one part of their habit. What colors does the full habit combine?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Ignatius Loyola (later ladder) or Bernard of Clairvaux — a founder answering an ecclesial crisis with a specific new form of life. Honest on the ROSARY tradition (Alan de la Roche, 15th c.) vs. actual bead-prayer development. Honest on the Dominican-inquisitorial role as historical complication — the good and the difficult in the same order.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the Albigensian Crusade and the Inquisition. Theology owns Dominic's founding STORY, the black-and-white habit, and the Michelangelo-arca connection. GEOGRAPHY owns Bologna as a place.

name: Thomas Aquinas: the ox of Sicily and 'all I have written seems like straw'
scope: T1: THOMAS AQUINAS is born c. 1225 in the family castle of ROCCASECCA in the Kingdom of Sicily (in what is now Lazio, Italy), youngest son of the Count of Aquino; his family wants him to become abbot of the great Benedictine monastery of MONTE CASSINO nearby, a position that would honor the family name. T2: at 19 (c. 1244), studying at the University of Naples, Thomas instead joins the new mendicant DOMINICAN order — a shock to his aristocratic family; his brothers kidnap him on the road to Rome and IMPRISON him in the family castle for A YEAR, trying to change his mind; his sister slips him books; his brothers even (per one tradition) send a courtesan to his cell — he drives her out with a burning brand from the fire, then falls asleep and receives from angels a girdle of chastity. T3: released, Thomas travels north and studies under ALBERT THE GREAT (Albertus Magnus) at Paris and Cologne; because Thomas is huge and heavy and speaks very little, his fellow students nickname him the DUMB OX; Albert, hearing this, rebukes them: 'You call him the Dumb Ox; I tell you that this Dumb Ox will one day fill the world with his BELLOWING.' T4: Thomas becomes the greatest theologian of the age, writing (mostly at Paris) the SUMMA CONTRA GENTILES and beginning c. 1265 the SUMMA THEOLOGIAE — a systematic exposition of Christian teaching structured as thousands of questions with objections, replies, and citations, engaging Aristotle (whom he calls simply 'THE PHILOSOPHER'), the Muslim commentator Averroes ('THE COMMENTATOR'), and the church fathers. T5: on December 6, 1273, during Mass at the Dominican priory in NAPLES, Thomas has an experience so overwhelming he STOPS WRITING the Summa Theologiae mid-question (III q.90, on penance); when his secretary Reginald of Piperno begs him to continue, Thomas answers: 'RAYMOND, I CANNOT — ALL THAT I HAVE WRITTEN SEEMS LIKE STRAW TO ME COMPARED TO WHAT I HAVE SEEN' (Bartholomew of Capua's canonization testimony, 1319). He never writes another word of the Summa. Called by the pope four months later to attend the Council of Lyons, he hits his head on a low-hanging tree branch on the road, becomes ill, and dies at the Cistercian abbey of FOSSANOVA on March 7, 1274, aged about 49; the Summa Theologiae is left unfinished — his brother Dominicans complete it later from his earlier writings as the SUPPLEMENT. Further rungs: the Aristotle-integration as revolutionary (aristotle's works had returned to Europe through Arabic translation in the 12th century); Aquinas' FIVE WAYS proofs of God's existence (Summa I q.2 a.3); the account by Bartholomew that Thomas as a boy at Monte Cassino repeatedly asked his teachers 'WHAT IS GOD?'; the canonization in 1323 by John XXII; the modern encyclical Aeterni Patris (1879) making Thomism the semi-official Catholic philosophy.
source: Grokipedia 'Thomas Aquinas' (browser); Bartholomew of Capua, testimony at Aquinas's canonization proceedings, 1319; William of Tocco, Vita Sancti Thomae Aquinatis, c. 1323; Wikipedia 'Thomas Aquinas'; primary: Bartholomew's testimony (in the Acta Sanctorum) for the 'straw' quote; Summa Theologiae itself.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T5 — 'ALL I HAVE WRITTEN SEEMS LIKE STRAW' and Thomas STOPPING the Summa Theologiae unfinished after a single mystical experience at Mass. Parents who studied any philosophy know Aquinas as an intellectual monument; almost none know he QUIT MID-SENTENCE. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Roccasecca for Aquino (his family's town, related — a real mine); at T2 swap the Dominican order-shock for Franciscan (the other new mendicant order; also a family-scandalizing choice — a real mine); at T3 swap the DUMB OX nickname's issuer (Albertus is right; fellow students named him, ALBERT defended); at T5 swap the Summa's stopping-question (it stopped at III q.90 on penance — this is documented precisely) and swap 'straw' for 'chaff' / 'ashes' / 'dust'. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T5 stem — 'After his experience at Mass in Naples, Thomas told his secretary that all he had written seemed like WHAT compared to what he had seen?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Snorri Sturluson, Cicero, or Confucius — a great mind's specific biographical shape. The mystical Naples experience is preserved by NAMED witnesses at the canonization inquiry — kids can trace it. His nickname (Dumb Ox), his weight (he was famously enormous), his death age (49), his unfinished work — all specific and true.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY owns Aquinas as a reasoning-figure (Five Ways as reasoning moves — see philosophy bank). Theology owns the LIFE STORY: the kidnapping, the Dumb Ox nickname, the Naples experience, the unfinished Summa. GEOGRAPHY owns Roccasecca, Naples, and Fossanova.

name: Hildegard of Bingen: visions since age three and the illuminated Scivias
scope: T1: HILDEGARD is born 1098 in the Rhineland village of BERMERSHEIM, tenth child of a noble family; she says she has seen visions of light since AGE THREE — 'a light so great my soul quaked' (Vita Sanctae Hildegardis, dictated to her secretary Volmar). At age eight her family gives her as a TITHE (a tenth-child offering) to the anchoress JUTTA at DISIBODENBERG monastery, where she is walled into an anchorage-cell to spend her life. T2: Jutta dies in 1136; Hildegard, now 38, becomes prioress of the little group of nuns that has gathered at Disibodenberg; five years later, in 1141, she receives what she calls the LIVING LIGHT commanding her to 'WRITE what you see and hear' — she doubts, becomes ill in bed, and only recovers when she obeys, calling in her friend Volmar as scribe. T3: over ten years (1141-1151) she writes SCIVIAS ('Know the Ways [of the Lord]') — twenty-six visions with theological commentaries; the book is illuminated in her own scriptorium with images extraordinary for their period: cosmic wheels, a mother church holding the world, GOD AS A GREAT EGG containing the universe. When Pope Eugenius III himself hears extracts read at the Synod of Trier in 1147-48, he officially approves her prophetic gift — making her the only medieval woman with formal papal endorsement to write, preach, and publish. T4: Hildegard also composes over 70 pieces of LITURGICAL MUSIC (an unusually large surviving output for the period), collected as the SYMPHONIA ARMONIE CELESTIUM REVELATIONUM; her Latin poetry is set to soaring melismatic chant; she writes a MYSTERY PLAY, Ordo Virtutum ('Play of the Virtues'), that is the earliest surviving morality play in Europe. She also writes two works of NATURAL MEDICINE — Physica (on plants, animals, minerals, elements) and Causae et Curae (on the human body and diseases) — full of remedies for everyday ailments; some of them (fennel for digestion, spelt as a strengthening grain) are still marketed in Germany as 'Hildegard cookies' and teas. T5: in her seventies and eighties Hildegard undertakes four PREACHING TOURS along the Rhine — an unheard-of thing for a woman — addressing not just monks and nuns but crowds of laypeople and secular clergy in cities like Trier, Cologne, and Kirchheim. She quarrels with her own archbishop of Mainz over the burial of an excommunicated nobleman in her cemetery and has her convent placed under INTERDICT (no bells, no sung Mass) for six months; she wins the fight in the end and the interdict is lifted. She dies September 17, 1179, aged 81; witnesses report that as she died TWO GREAT BEAMS OF LIGHT appeared in the sky, crossing over her cell (Vita). She was formally canonized only in 2012 by Benedict XVI and named a DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH the same year — one of only four women ever given that title. Further rungs: Hildegard's correspondence — over 400 letters survive, exchanged with popes, emperors (Frederick Barbarossa), abbots, and ordinary petitioners; her word LINGUA IGNOTA — an artificial language of 1,011 invented words with a matching invented alphabet; the RUPERTSBERG convent she founded 1150 near Bingen; the modern rediscovery — the group Sequentia's 1990s recordings of her music selling worldwide.
source: Grokipedia 'Hildegard of Bingen' (browser); Vita Sanctae Hildegardis by Gottfried of Disibodenberg (started c. 1174, completed by Theoderich of Echternach c. 1187); Wikipedia 'Hildegard of Bingen'; primary: her own Scivias preface and letter to Volmar for the 'Living Light' quote; the Symphonia; Physica; Causae et Curae.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T4 — Hildegard wrote 70+ pieces of MUSIC (still recorded today, still sold), the earliest morality PLAY, and MEDICAL manuals — and preached openly in the 1150s-70s. Modern audiences find the range shocking. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Bermersheim / Disibodenberg / Bingen (all real, all in her biography — Bingen is where she founded her SECOND convent, Rupertsberg; Disibodenberg is where she was walled in as a girl); at T3 swap the pope-approver (Eugenius III is right; Innocent III / Gregory VII are traps); at T4 swap her medical remedies (fennel and spelt are right — real Hildegard recommendations); at T5 swap the Doctor-of-the-Church count (four women — Teresa of Avila, Catherine of Siena, Therese of Lisieux, Hildegard). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T4 stem — 'Besides theology, Hildegard produced substantial work in TWO other very different fields — one to be sung, one to be dosed. What two?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell the Norse volva (seeress) chanting the Voluspa, or the Sibyl of Cumae writing on leaves — a woman authorized as visionary in a specifically female voice. Not softened, not romanticized; the anchorite-cell start at age 8 and the archbishop-quarrel at 78 are kept in.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns 12th-c. Rhineland politics and the Investiture Controversy. Theology owns Hildegard's LIFE and works — the visions, Scivias, Symphonia, medicine, preaching tours. GEOGRAPHY owns the Rhine as a place.

name: Bernard of Clairvaux and the Second Crusade sermon at Vezelay
scope: T1: BERNARD is born 1090 near Dijon in Burgundy; at age 22 (1112) he arrives at the struggling new reformed monastery of CITEAUX with 30 companions — his own brothers, cousins, and friends whom he has persuaded to renounce noble careers and follow him. This mass entry saves Citeaux, which had been dying out. T2: three years later Abbot Stephen Harding sends the 25-year-old Bernard to found a new daughter-house in the wilderness of the CLAIR VAL ('bright valley') on the Aube — CLAIRVAUX; there Bernard, tall, gaunt with fasting, becomes for the next 38 years the most influential churchman in Europe, though never rising above the office of abbot. His writings, especially the sermons on the SONG OF SONGS (86 sermons over 18 years, unfinished at his death), become foundational for medieval mysticism. T3: on Christmas Day 1144 the Muslim atabeg Zengi captures the crusader county of EDESSA (the first major crusader-state loss in the East); Pope Eugenius III — himself a Cistercian and Bernard's own former pupil — commissions Bernard to preach a new crusade. T4: on Easter Sunday, March 31, 1146, at VEZELAY in Burgundy, Bernard preaches the SECOND CRUSADE from a wooden platform to a great crowd on the hillside outside the basilica of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine (the church is too small); KING LOUIS VII of France is there with Queen ELEANOR OF AQUITAINE; the crowd shouts 'CRUCES! CRUCES!' ('crosses! crosses!'). Bernard runs out of pre-cut cloth crosses to distribute and tears his own MONASTIC HABIT into strips to make more. Odo of Deuil, the king's chaplain, is the eyewitness ('De profectione Ludovici VII in Orientem', 1148). T5: the crusade Bernard preaches becomes a disaster — the German army under Conrad III is nearly wiped out by Turks in Anatolia; the French army suffers catastrophic losses; the siege of Damascus in 1148 fails in four days. Bernard's reputation is damaged; he writes a somber apology (De Consideratione II.1) that God has 'not shown him the reason' for the failure. He dies at Clairvaux August 20, 1153, having sent monks out to found 68 daughter-houses of his own abbey (the CISTERCIAN white-habited order spread to 340 abbeys across Europe by 1200); he is canonized 1174 and named a DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH in 1830 as the 'DOCTOR MELLIFLUUS' ('honey-flowing doctor') for his prose. Further rungs: Bernard's role at the Council of Sens 1141 condemning Peter Abelard's theology (a bitter, complicated moment — kept as complication); his correspondence with Hildegard of Bingen ('the trumpet of the Lord'); his writings on the Virgin Mary shaping medieval devotion; the modern hymn 'O Sacred Head, Now Wounded' derived from a Latin poem attributed to Bernard (probably by his followers, actually).

name: Julian of Norwich: 'all shall be well'
scope: T1: in May 1373, in the English city of NORWICH — a plague-stricken port on the eastern coast — a woman about 30 years old lies dying of a mysterious illness; her mother and a priest are at her bedside, and the priest is holding a crucifix in front of her fading vision. T2: on May 8 or 13, 1373, over the course of about five hours between four and nine in the morning, she experiences SIXTEEN VISIONS (or 'SHEWINGS') — beginning when the crucifix in front of her seems to bleed under the crown of thorns; the visions include Christ's Passion in extraordinary physical detail, the mother of Jesus, and images she calls 'PARABLES': a NUT the size of a hazelnut in the palm of her hand containing 'all that is made' — 'so little that I marvelled how it might last, for methought it might suddenly have fallen to nought for littleness. And I was answered ... It lasteth, and ever shall last, for God loveth it.' T3: she recovers, and over the next 20 years writes down and repeatedly deepens what she saw — first a SHORT TEXT (soon after the visions) and then a LONG TEXT (c. 1393). Around 1400 she moves into a small anchorage-cell attached to the wall of the parish church of ST JULIAN, Conisford, Norwich — from which we get the name we call her by. Nothing is known of her birth name. T4: the LONG TEXT contains what has become perhaps the most quoted line in English mysticism: 'ALL SHALL BE WELL, AND ALL SHALL BE WELL, AND ALL MANNER OF THING SHALL BE WELL' (Revelations of Divine Love, ch. 27 — as Christ's reply to her about sin and suffering); the text also includes a full chapter (ch. 60) speaking of Jesus as MOTHER — 'as truly as God is our Father, so truly is God our Mother' — an image drawn from earlier Cistercian sources but developed with unprecedented depth. Her Revelations is the FIRST BOOK WRITTEN IN ENGLISH BY A WOMAN whose name (Julian, whatever her true baptismal name) we know. T5: her anchorage cell has a small window — a 'HAGIOSCOPE' — that opens into the parish church for daily Mass, and another window opening onto the street. Through the street window she gives spiritual counsel to visitors. The Norfolk visionary MARGERY KEMPE, herself far more turbulent, records visiting Julian in Norwich c. 1413 in her own Book (also the first autobiography in English — by a laywoman); Margery says she sat with Julian for 'many days' talking about her own visions and left with encouragement. Julian is thought to have died sometime after 1416 (a bequest to her by that name is recorded that year). She was never formally canonized by Rome; the Church of England formally added her to its calendar in 1980; the Catholic Church honors her but by common tradition rather than formal cause. Further rungs: T.S. Eliot's Four Quartets (Little Gidding, 1942) ending 'And all shall be well, and / All manner of thing shall be well / When the tongues of flame are in-folded / Into the crowned knot of fire / And the fire and the rose are one' — direct Julian quotation; the ANCHORAGE cell rebuilt after WWII bomb damage, visitors still visit the site; the parable of the LORD AND THE SERVANT (ch. 51) — a long allegory about a servant falling into a pit and being lifted up.

framing_note: DINNER TEST: T2 — the HAZELNUT vision — 'a little thing, the quantity of an hazelnut ... it is all that is made'. It's the single most famous image in all Julian, and grade-10 kids can hold it easily. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap the city (Norwich right; Canterbury / York / Ely all real, all English cathedral cities); at T2 swap the year (1373 is documented in the Long Text preface); at T3 swap the church (St Julian, Conisford is right; St Peter Mancroft / Norwich Cathedral are traps); at T4 swap the famous quote's exact form — 'all shall be well and all shall be well and all manner of thing shall be well' has THREE parts (kids often shorten it); at T5 swap Margery Kempe for another female medieval mystic (Bridget of Sweden, Catherine of Siena — both real, both nearby in time). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T2 stem — 'Julian saw in her hand something no bigger than a hazelnut, and understood it to be ALL THAT IS MADE. What was the object she saw?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell the volva's prophecy in the Voluspa or the Delphic pythia's utterance — a woman's visionary text preserved verbatim, quoted by later writers across centuries. Honest on 'we do not know her real name' — Julian is the name of the CHURCH she was anchored at. Not softened; the illness at 30, the anchorage window, the anchorage rebuild after bombing.

name: Catherine of Siena writing to popes
scope: T1: CATERINA BENINCASA — Catherine — is born in Siena in 1347 (the year the Black Death arrives in Italy), 24th of 25 children of the dyer Jacopo Benincasa; her twin sister dies in infancy. At about age SIX, walking home with her brother, Catherine looks up at the sky above the Basilica of San Domenico in Siena and sees a vision of Christ in papal robes blessing her; she runs home changed. T2: at seven she privately vows virginity; when her family later tries to make her marry her dead sister's widower, she CUTS OFF her HAIR and refuses food; her family relents and lets her become a Dominican TERTIARY (a laywoman under Dominican rule) at 16 — the mantellate wear the Dominican black-and-white but live at home. She spends the next three years locked in a small room of her family's house praying, speaking only to her confessor, in what she later called her 'CELL of self-knowledge'. T3: at 21 (c. 1368) she has what she calls her MYSTICAL MARRIAGE to Christ, with a ring visible only to her — after which she leaves the room and begins nursing plague and leprosy patients at Siena's hospital of Santa Maria della Scala; she also begins writing LETTERS (nearly 400 survive) — dictated aloud to secretaries, since she was likely illiterate at the time (she reportedly learned to read and write miraculously in her twenties). The letters go to popes, cardinals, kings, mercenary captains (like the Englishman John Hawkwood, whom she scolds for fighting Christians), plague sufferers, and her own disciples. T4: her greatest political achievement: in 1376 she TRAVELS TO AVIGNON — where the popes had been living for nearly 70 years, effectively under French royal influence — and confronts Pope GREGORY XI face to face, urging him to return the papal see to ROME as he had privately vowed to do. Gregory returns to Rome on January 17, 1377 — largely (in tradition) at Catherine's insistence, ending the 'AVIGNON PAPACY' (1309-1377). T5: after Gregory's death in 1378, the disputed election of Urban VI splits the Church in the WESTERN SCHISM, with a rival pope at Avignon; Catherine writes furiously in support of the Roman pope; she moves to Rome and dies there on April 29, 1380, aged only 33, worn out by extreme fasting (in her last months she reportedly could only ingest the Eucharist); her Dialogue of Divine Providence (dictated c. 1377-78) survives as a mystical dialogue between the Soul and God the Father. She was canonized in 1461, declared PATRON of ITALY (with Francis of Assisi) in 1939, and named a DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH in 1970 by Paul VI — the FIRST WOMAN so named (with Teresa of Avila the same year). In 1999 John Paul II named her CO-PATRON OF EUROPE. Her HEAD is preserved as relic at San Domenico in Siena; her body at Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome. Further rungs: the STIGMATA — Catherine reported receiving the marks in 1375 at Pisa, but by her request they were invisible to others during her lifetime, becoming visible after her death (Raymond of Capua's testimony); Raymond of Capua as her confessor, biographer (Legenda Maior, c. 1385), and later Master General of the Dominicans; her scolding letter to Gregory XI: 'BE A MAN, father, not a coward.'

Suzanne Noffke, 4 vols); the Dialogue of Divine Providence, c. 1377-78; Wikipedia 'Catherine of Siena'; primary: her Letters (Letter 206 to Gregory XI for the 'be a man' phrasing) and the Dialogue.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T5 — 'BE A MAN, FATHER, NOT A COWARD' — Catherine, a 29-year-old unlettered dyer's daughter, writing that to the pope. It's her actual text (Letter 206, to Gregory XI); the boldness stuns modern readers. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Siena for Assisi (real, other central-Italian saint town); at T2 swap Dominican tertiary for Franciscan tertiary (real, other order-with-laypeople); at T3 swap Santa Maria della Scala for other real Sienese sites; at T4 swap Avignon for Anagni (real, earlier papal humiliation site) / Rome; at T5 swap her Doctor-of-the-Church year (1970 with Teresa is right; other later women get the title too — she was one of the FIRST TWO). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T4 stem — 'Catherine of Siena traveled in 1376 to a city in France where the popes had been living for nearly seventy years, and persuaded the pope to move his court back to Rome. What was that city?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Antigone confronting Creon or Deborah calling Barak — a woman speaking with authority to a ruler in a specific documented setting. Honest: her stigmata were reportedly invisible in her lifetime by her own request (per Raymond); her fasting was extreme and likely contributed to her early death at 33.

name: Joan of Arc: Domremy, the voices, and the siege of Orleans
scope: T1: JEANNE D'ARC (Joan of Arc) is born c. 1412 in the village of DOMREMY on the Meuse in eastern France, daughter of the farmer Jacques d'Arc and Isabelle Romee; France is in the disastrous 90th year of the Hundred Years' War, with the north (including Paris) under English occupation and the Dauphin Charles uncrowned, holding only the south from Bourges. T2: at 13, in her father's garden at Domremy, Joan begins to hear VOICES that identify themselves as the ARCHANGEL MICHAEL, SAINT CATHERINE (of Alexandria), and SAINT MARGARET (of Antioch); over four years the voices become insistent that she must go to the Dauphin, drive the English out of France, and see Charles crowned at REIMS (the traditional coronation city, then under English/Burgundian control). T3: at 16 she persuades a relative to take her to the nearest French garrison at VAUCOULEURS; Robert de Baudricourt, the commander, twice refuses her and eventually agrees to send her with an escort — she cuts her hair short, dresses in men's clothing for the 11-day cross-country ride through enemy territory, and arrives at the Dauphin's court at CHINON castle in late February 1429. Charles, testing her, has himself dressed as a commoner and hides among his courtiers — Joan walks straight past the impostor on the throne to Charles and identifies him. T4: given command of a relief force, she rides to besieged ORLEANS on April 29, 1429 — the city has been under English siege for six months, its fall would open the road to the Loire and end French independence. Wearing WHITE ARMOR and carrying a WHITE BANNER embroidered with lilies and the names JESUS MARIA, she leads assaults on the English fortresses. On May 7, attacking the LES TOURELLES fort at the bridge, she is struck by a CROSSBOW BOLT through her SHOULDER above her breastplate — pulls out the bolt herself, returns to the assault by evening; the English abandon the siege the next day. Nine days later she leads the army to victory at Patay; on July 17, 1429, she stands beside Charles at his coronation in REIMS CATHEDRAL. T5: captured by Burgundians at COMPIEGNE on May 23, 1430 when the town gate was closed too early behind her rearguard, Joan is SOLD to the English for 10,000 livres and tried at ROUEN by a French ecclesiastical court under Bishop Pierre Cauchon (an English partisan). The trial lasts four months (January-May 1431). The 70 charges against her focus on her VOICES, her wearing of MEN'S CLOTHING, and her refusal to submit her voices' authority to the Church. She is condemned, briefly recants, then resumes men's clothes in prison (some accounts say because her guards had removed the women's clothes she had been given). On May 30, 1431, aged about 19, she is burned at the stake in the OLD MARKET SQUARE (Place du Vieux-Marche) of Rouen. She asks to hold a CROSS through the flames; an English soldier makes her a small one from two sticks; a Dominican, Isambard de la Pierre, brings a proper crucifix from a nearby church and HOLDS IT UP for her to see. Her last recorded words are 'JESUS' repeated. The executioner Geoffroy Therage later confessed he 'feared he was damned' for burning a saint. Her ashes are cast into the Seine. Charles VII orders a retrial in 1456 that clears her name; Joan is canonized in 1920 by Benedict XV and named a co-patron of France. Further rungs: the SWORD from behind the altar at Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois that Joan asked for and reportedly received (found where she said it would be, buried behind the altar); the banner that she preferred to her sword; the CHARLES VII coronation itself on July 17, 1429 — the culminating goal of her mission; the 1456 nullification trial where 115 witnesses (many from Domremy) testified; the tree at Domremy called 'l'Arbre des Fees' that childhood-Joan danced around at (raised as an accusation in the trial).
