framing_note: DINNER TEST: T5 — the CROSS MADE FROM TWO STICKS by an English soldier for Joan to hold as the flames rose (nullification testimony, Isambard de la Pierre's deposition). One of the most piercing details in medieval history. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T2 swap the three named voices (Michael, Catherine, Margaret is right; Michael/Gabriel/Raphael is a trap — those are archangels but only Michael appears in her voices); at T3 swap Chinon for Bourges (real Charles VII court city, wrong for the identification scene); at T4 swap the arrow-strike location (shoulder is right, above the breastplate; through the thigh is Louis IX's crusader wound, a trap); at T5 swap Rouen for Compiegne (site of capture, not execution) / Paris; swap the execution square Old Market for Place de Greve (real Paris execution site, wrong city). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T5 stem — 'At the stake in Rouen, Joan asked to see a cross. What did an English soldier improvise for her?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Cuchulainn tied standing to a stone facing his enemies, or Roland dying under his sword Durendal at Roncesvalles — a warrior figure named, weapon named, wound named, quote named, last-moment gesture named. Joan is a HISTORICAL figure with VERBATIM TRIAL TRANSCRIPTS (unique among medieval saints), so precision is possible and required. No 'God's warrior' triumphal frame; no 'delusional peasant girl' smug-atheist frame — the trial and the nullification are the double sources.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the Hundred Years' War, the Dauphin/King Charles VII's reign, and the political events (siege of Orleans, coronation at Reims, capture at Compiegne). Theology owns Joan's VOICES, her cross-of-sticks moment, her nullification-declared sanctity, and her canonization STORY. GEOGRAPHY owns Domremy, Orleans, Reims, and Rouen as places.

name: Joan of Arc: the trial, the flames, and 'hold the cross high'
scope: T1: after her capture at Compiegne in May 1430, Joan is held for months in various castles (Beaurevoir, Rouen); at Beaurevoir she jumps from a 60-foot tower window trying to escape (or trying to warn the besieged Compiegne — accounts differ), landing without permanent injury but nearly killing herself; her voices later scold her for the jump. T2: bought by the English in November 1430 for 10,000 livres tournois, she is delivered to ROUEN and to Bishop PIERRE CAUCHON — a French bishop of Beauvais, loyal to the English, ambitious for the archbishopric of Rouen — who convenes an ecclesiastical trial on charges of heresy. The court includes 131 clerics over the trial's duration, mostly from the University of Paris (then loyal to the English regency). T3: the trial runs January 9 to May 30, 1431. Joan is held in a MILITARY prison (not the ecclesiastical prison that church law would have required), guarded by five English soldiers even in her cell, and never allowed the female companions or the priest-confessor that church law required. She wears MEN'S CLOTHES tied with cords through the tunic to the hose — later argued to be a protection against sexual assault by her guards. The trial records preserve HER EXACT WORDS across 27 sessions of interrogation; her answers, given without counsel, at 19 years old, unlettered, become one of the great witness-documents of the medieval period. Asked whether she knows she is in God's grace, she answers, 'If I am not, may God put me there; if I am, may God so keep me' — an answer the theologians recognize as brilliantly avoiding the trap. T4: on May 24, 1431, taken to the cemetery of Saint-Ouen and shown the stake, Joan collapses and briefly RECANTS, signing an abjuration (a mark, since she was largely unlettered), agreeing to wear women's clothes. Back in her cell she resumes men's clothes within days (one account says the guards took the women's clothes; another that her voices reproached her). Cauchon declares her a RELAPSED HERETIC on May 28, and the sentence of burning is confirmed. T5: on Wednesday morning May 30, 1431, Joan is taken in a cart to the OLD MARKET SQUARE (Place du Vieux-Marche) in Rouen. A high plaster STAKE has been built with a placard reading 'HERETIC, RELAPSED, APOSTATE, IDOLATER' above where her head will be. She weeps as she is tied to the stake, but when the fire is lit she calls out for a CROSS. The English soldier makes her a small one from two sticks; the Dominican Isambard de la Pierre brings the processional crucifix from the church of Saint-Sauveur and stays close, holding it up to her; witnesses at the 1456 nullification testify that Joan repeatedly cried, 'JESUS! HOLD THE CROSS HIGH SO I MAY SEE IT THROUGH THE FLAMES!' She dies calling 'Jesus'; her ashes are gathered by the executioner Geoffroy Therage and thrown into the Seine so no relics can be preserved. Twenty-five years later Charles VII orders the RETRIAL OF NULLIFICATION (1455-56); 115 witnesses, including surviving villagers from Domremy who had known her as a child, are called; the sentence of 1431 is annulled and Joan declared innocent. She is canonized in 1920. Further rungs: her chosen banner over her chosen sword; her mother Isabelle Romee traveling to Rome in her 70s and appearing personally before the nullification tribunal; the 20th-c. discovery of her precise physical descriptions in the trial (short, dark hair, husky voice); the transcript's status as unique among medieval saints — no other has a verbatim record of her own words at this length.
source: Grokipedia 'Joan of Arc' + 'Trial of Joan of Arc' (browser); Trial of Condemnation, Rouen 1431 (verbatim Latin transcript with French vernacular Joan-answers); Trial of Nullification, 1456 (115 depositions); Wikipedia 'Trial of Joan of Arc' and 'Retrial of Joan of Arc'; primary: the two trial transcripts.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T5 — 'HOLD THE CROSS HIGH SO I MAY SEE IT THROUGH THE FLAMES' — Joan's actual cry at the stake, recorded by multiple named witnesses at the 1456 nullification. And the executioner GEOFFROY THERAGE later saying he 'feared he was damned' for having burned a saint (his exact deposition survives). DISTRACTOR MINE: at T3 swap Joan's brilliant grace-answer for other famous saint quotes; at T4 swap the recantation-then-relapse (some know only the recantation, some only the relapse — the twenty-first-century picture requires both); at T5 swap the executioner name (Geoffroy Therage is right, documented in the trial supplement); swap Isambard de la Pierre for Martin Ladvenu (another real Dominican who accompanied her — a real mine); swap the ashes-in-the-Seine (right — deliberately to prevent relic-cult). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T5 stem — 'As the flames rose, Joan called out for someone to do WHAT with the cross Isambard held near her?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told with the exact restraint the historical evidence permits — Joan's actual words survive, so precision replaces piety. This is a documented judicial murder of a 19-year-old with a full trial transcript and a full retrial transcript; the story stands on its own without moralizing gloss. The 20-year gap between condemnation and nullification is honestly kept.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the political and military context (Hundred Years' War end-phase; Cauchon's political motivations). Theology owns Joan's trial testimony, the stake, and the nullification. GEOGRAPHY owns Rouen and the Old Market Square as places.

name: John Hus at Constance: 'in a hundred years God will raise up a man'
scope: T1: JAN HUS is a Czech priest, rector of the CHARLES UNIVERSITY at PRAGUE (the oldest university in central Europe, founded 1348), and preacher at the BETHLEHEM CHAPEL in Prague where he preaches in the CZECH vernacular to congregations of thousands — a radical practice in a Latin-only church world. T2: influenced by the English reformer JOHN WYCLIFFE (d. 1384), whose works had reached Bohemia through the marriage of King Richard II of England to Anne of Bohemia, Hus preaches against the sale of INDULGENCES (Pope John XXIII's 1412 sale to fund a crusade), the wealth of the church, and the veneration of pope-as-Antichrist when the pope acts contrary to Christ; he defends communion in BOTH kinds (bread AND wine to the laity, not just the priest — the 'utraquist' position) that becomes the identity-mark of his Czech followers. T3: excommunicated in 1411, Hus takes refuge in southern Bohemia and writes his DE ECCLESIA ('On the Church'); in 1414 he agrees to travel to the COUNCIL OF CONSTANCE (called by Emperor Sigismund to end the WESTERN SCHISM — three rival popes at the time) under an IMPERIAL SAFE-CONDUCT to explain his views. Sigismund's safe-conduct is famously violated: Hus is arrested within a month of arrival (November 1414) and held for eight months in a dungeon by the Rhine, at times chained to a wall. T4: at his TRIAL before the council on June 7-8, 1415, Hus is not allowed to explain his views but only to recant a list of extracted propositions; he refuses because he does not accept that some of them accurately state his teaching. He is condemned as a heretic, DEGRADED from the priesthood (his tonsure re-cut with scissors in the shape of a paper crown, his liturgical robes stripped off), and handed to the SECULAR ARM for execution. As they place a PAPER CROWN painted with three devils on his head, he says, 'My Lord Jesus Christ for my sake wore a much heavier and more painful crown of thorns.' T5: on July 6, 1415, at a place outside the city walls of CONSTANCE (called the 'Bruel'), Hus is tied to a stake, faggots piled around him to the chin, straw mixed among them. Offered a chance to recant even now, he answers, 'God is my witness that the things charged against me I never preached. In the same truth of the Gospel which I have written, taught, and preached, drawing upon the sayings and positions of the holy doctors, I am ready to die today.' As the fire is lit he cries, 'Christ, thou son of the living God, have mercy upon me!' — repeating it as the flames overtake him. Tradition preserves a prophecy attributed to him on the way to the stake or in prison: 'AFTER A HUNDRED YEARS GOD WILL RAISE UP A MAN whose calls for reform cannot be suppressed' — a prophecy Bohemians later applied to MARTIN LUTHER (who nailed his 95 theses in 1517, 102 years after Hus's burning). Luther explicitly claimed Hus as his forerunner: 'We are all Hussites without knowing it.' The Council of Constance also had Wycliffe's bones dug up and burned. Hus's execution triggered the HUSSITE WARS (1419-1434) in Bohemia — the first successful mass Christian resistance to a papal crusading army in medieval history. Further rungs: the historical origin of his name — 'Hus' means 'GOOSE' in Czech; on his way to the stake he reportedly punned, 'Today you roast a goose, but from the ashes will rise a swan you cannot roast' — Luther's followers took the swan as a Reformation symbol (many Lutheran churches have a swan on the pulpit); the Bethlehem Chapel destroyed and rebuilt as a reconstruction in Prague; Hus commemorated in the Old Town Square of Prague by a large sculpture unveiled 1915 for the 500th anniversary of his burning.
source: Grokipedia 'Jan Hus' + 'Council of Constance' (browser); Peter of Mladonovice, Relatio de Magistro Johanne Hus, c. 1415-16 (eyewitness account by Hus's own secretary at Constance); Wikipedia 'Jan Hus' and 'Hussite Wars'; primary: Peter of Mladonovice's Relatio for the trial and execution scenes; Hus's own De Ecclesia.
framing_note: DINNER TEST: T5 — the GOOSE/SWAN pun. 'Hus' actually MEANS goose in Czech; Hus reportedly said, 'today you roast a goose, but from the ashes will rise a swan you cannot roast'; Martin Luther a century later was called that swan and the swan became a Lutheran symbol. Kids find the word-play thrilling and it's true. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Charles University Prague for Wittenberg (Luther's later university, real trap); swap Bethlehem Chapel for Wittenberg's Castle Church; at T2 swap Wycliffe for Wesley (18th-c., wrong era) / Wyclif spelling variants; at T3 swap the safe-conduct issuer (Emperor Sigismund is right; the pope did NOT issue it); at T4 swap the paper-crown detail (three devils painted on it — this is documented at Constance); at T5 swap the '100 years' timing — the prophecy is c. 1415 and Luther's 95 theses 1517, so 102 years — precise. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T5 stem — 'Hus's Czech surname means the same thing as one common bird. What bird?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Socrates in his cell drinking the hemlock — a teacher walking clear-eyed to execution because he will not recant. Honest on the SAFE-CONDUCT betrayal — a major medieval scandal; honest that his execution TRIGGERED the Hussite Wars (military resistance, not passive martyrdom). The Luther-swan connection is a real Lutheran iconographic tradition that persists today.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the Council of Constance's political work (ending Western Schism, electing Martin V), the Hussite Wars, and Sigismund's reign. Theology owns Hus's TRIAL and MARTYRDOM story and the goose-swan tradition. GEOGRAPHY owns Constance as a place.

name: Thomas More: 'the King's good servant, but God's first'
scope: T1: THOMAS MORE, born 1478, London lawyer, humanist scholar (author of UTOPIA, 1516 — the coined word), friend of ERASMUS, becomes in 1529 LORD CHANCELLOR of England under KING HENRY VIII — the first layman to hold that highest legal office. T2: More resists Henry's demand for a divorce from Catherine of Aragon and Henry's declaration of himself SUPREME HEAD OF THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND (Act of Supremacy, 1534). More is not a preacher against these acts; he simply REFUSES to sign the OATH OF SUPREMACY. He resigns as Chancellor in 1532 and lives quietly at his Chelsea house with his large learned family — his beloved daughter MARGARET ROPER, herself a Greek and Latin scholar, is the equal of his sons in his household school. T3: refusing the oath in April 1534, More is imprisoned in the TOWER OF LONDON — first in comfortable quarters, then in worsening conditions; he writes A DIALOGUE OF COMFORT AGAINST TRIBULATION and other works while imprisoned. Fifteen months of interrogation, visits from his daughter Margaret, appeals from his old friends fail to move him. He is tried in Westminster Hall on July 1, 1535; the crucial testimony is perjured (Sir Richard Rich claims More told him privately Parliament could not make Henry supreme head — More denies it under oath); More is condemned by a jury who reach their verdict in FIFTEEN MINUTES. Only after the verdict does he speak openly against the Act of Supremacy. T4: on July 6, 1535 (five days after conviction — the sentence commuted from hanging-drawing-and-quartering to simple beheading), More walks to the scaffold on TOWER HILL in London. The scaffold is rickety; he says to the officer helping him up, 'I pray you, Master Lieutenant, see me safe up: and for my coming down, let me shift for myself.' At the block he arranges his long BEARD carefully over the wood, saying (per Roper), 'This hath not offended the King.' His last recorded words, standing on the scaffold, are 'I DIE THE KING'S GOOD SERVANT, BUT GOD'S FIRST' (William Roper, Life of Sir Thomas More, c. 1557, his son-in-law's memoir; the Paris Newsletter of August 1535 gives 'I die the King's good servant and God's first'). He is beheaded with one stroke; his head is boiled in a pot and stuck on a pike on LONDON BRIDGE — the standard treatment for traitors. T5: his daughter MARGARET ROPER, twenty-nine years old, secretly bribes the bridge-keeper about a month later and RETRIEVES HER FATHER'S HEAD from the pike; she preserves it in spices for the rest of her life. When she dies in 1544, she is buried with his head in her arms in the ROPER VAULT at ST DUNSTAN's church in Canterbury, where it remains today (the church can be visited). Erasmus, hearing of More's death in the Netherlands, writes that in More 'England has lost one soul such as she has never had before, and shall not have again' (letter to Peter Tomiczki, August 1535). More was canonized in 1935 (with John Fisher, the bishop beheaded two weeks earlier); in 1980 the Church of England added More AND Fisher to its calendar (an unusual joint recognition). In 2000 John Paul II named More PATRON OF STATESMEN AND POLITICIANS. Further rungs: More's Utopia (1516) coining the word from Greek OU + TOPOS ('no place'); More's ROLE in prosecuting Protestants earlier as Chancellor — an honest complication (he had six Protestants burned at Smithfield during his tenure); his HAIR SHIRT worn secretly all his life, discovered by his family after his death; the film 'A Man for All Seasons' (1966) based on Robert Bolt's play, popularizing the story; the beard-arrangement quip preserved in Roper's Life.

The devotion is astonishing and true. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Antigone burying her brother against Creon's edict — a daughter defying royal terror to reclaim her father's body. HONEST: More persecuted Protestants during his Chancellorship — that goes in the further rungs, not softened. His last words are documented in TWO independent contemporary sources (Roper and the Paris Newsletter) — a rare double confirmation.

name: Ignatius Loyola: the cannonball at Pamplona and the vigil at Montserrat
scope: T1: INIGO LOPEZ DE LOYOLA (later Ignatius) is born 1491 at the Basque castle of LOYOLA, youngest of thirteen; he grows up a court page and then a soldier, vain of his good looks, wearing his hair long and his boots tight, dreaming of chivalric heroism from the romances of Amadis of Gaul. T2: on May 20, 1521, at the age of 30, defending the citadel of PAMPLONA against a French army during a Habsburg-Valois war, he refuses to surrender the position; a CANNONBALL passes between his legs, breaking one and wounding the other. The French, respecting his courage, treat him gently and carry him back to Loyola for his family to nurse. T3: bedridden for months, the shattered leg improperly set, Ignatius has his surgeons REBREAK and RESET it — twice — for cosmetic reasons (a protruding stump would ruin the fit of his fashionable boots); the second procedure nearly kills him. Recovering, he asks for chivalric romances to pass the time; his sister-in-law brings him the only two books in the castle: a life of CHRIST (Ludolph of Saxony's Vita Christi) and a book of SAINTS' LIVES (the Flos Sanctorum). He reads them for lack of anything else and finds himself dreaming as vividly of becoming a saint as he had dreamed of chivalric love — and the saint-dreams leave a lasting peace where the chivalric ones left restlessness. This becomes his first spiritual discovery: DISCERNMENT OF SPIRITS. T4: barely healed, in early 1522 he rides to the Marian shrine of MONTSERRAT in the mountains of Catalonia; he hangs his SWORD and DAGGER at Our Lady's altar as a knight-vigil, exchanges his fine clothes with a beggar (whose worn-out sackcloth he puts on), and walks to the nearby town of MANRESA. He intends to stay only briefly on his way to Jerusalem, but stays TEN MONTHS. T5: in a cave outside Manresa, over months of severe fasting and prayer that reduce him to skeletal thinness and near-suicide, Ignatius receives illuminations — the greatest by the river CARDONER (the 'Cardoner enlightenment') — that leave him understanding, in a single moment, more than years of study could have taught. He begins writing what will become the SPIRITUAL EXERCISES — a four-week guided retreat structured around meditations on sin, Christ's life, the Passion, and the Resurrection; he will spend the rest of his life refining it. Eventually he gathers COMPANIONS at the University of Paris — FRANCIS XAVIER, Peter Faber, Diego Lainez, Alfonso Salmeron, Nicolas Bobadilla, Simao Rodrigues — and on August 15, 1534, in a crypt at MONTMARTRE in Paris, the seven of them take vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience to the pope; from this vow grows the SOCIETY OF JESUS (formally approved by Paul III in 1540), whose members are known as JESUITS. Ignatius is elected first Superior General; the Society becomes the most intellectually and missionarily aggressive religious order of the Counter-Reformation, running schools and universities across Europe and sending missionaries (starting with Xavier) as far as INDIA, JAPAN, and later CHINA. Ignatius dies in Rome July 31, 1556. Further rungs: the AD MAIOREM DEI GLORIAM ('to the greater glory of God') motto shortened AMDG; Ignatius's insistence on obedience 'as a corpse' (perinde ac cadaver) — an image sometimes misquoted, always fierce; the Autobiography he dictated in his last years (unusual for a founder); his shrine at the Gesu church in Rome; the sword hung at Montserrat still shown as tradition.

That vanity-driven detail before his conversion is unforgettable and true (his own Autobiography). DISTRACTOR MINE: at T2 swap Pamplona (right) for other real Basque cities; at T4 swap Montserrat for MANRESA (which is where the Exercises are drafted — a real mine, adjacent); swap the sword-hanging with other real medieval knight-vigils; at T5 swap the seven companions (all real, all named), swap Montmartre (Paris, right) for other real Paris churches; swap 1534 for other real founding-year dates. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Cuchulainn's ristrad healing or Odysseus's scar from the boar — a warrior's body-history that becomes iconic for the man. Honest on the ferocious sacrifice — the boots, the sackcloth swap with a beggar, the ten months at Manresa nearly dying of self-denial, the sword at Our Lady's altar. Not romanticized; the Autobiography is honest about it and so is the ladder.

name: Teresa of Avila: the transverberation and reforming the Carmelites
scope: T1: TERESA DE CEPEDA Y AHUMADA is born in AVILA in Castile in 1515, third of a Jewish-converso merchant family (her paternal grandfather Juan Sanchez had been condemned by the Toledo Inquisition in 1485 for secretly practicing Judaism and reconciled — a fact Teresa kept private and modern historians only rediscovered from Inquisition records). She enters the CARMELITE convent of the Incarnation in Avila at age 20 (1535), where the observance is so relaxed that nuns keep their own servants, receive visitors freely in the parlor, and travel to family estates. For twenty-five years Teresa lives comfortably as a mediocre nun. T2: at about age 40, in front of a statue of the WOUNDED CHRIST BEING SCOURGED at the convent, she is pierced with sorrow at her own tepidity and undergoes what she calls her SECOND CONVERSION. Her prayer life deepens rapidly and unwillingly into MYSTICAL EXPERIENCES she does not seek — visions, locutions, and (starting c. 1560) ECSTASIES so intense that other nuns report having to hold her body down as she was carried upward off the ground in RAPTURES (Teresa's own Autobiography ch. 20, sober about the phenomenon and eager to be free of it). T3: the most famous of these experiences she calls the TRANSVERBERATION (Autobiography ch. 29, c. 1559): 'I saw in his hand a long GOLDEN SPEAR, and at the point of the iron there seemed to be a little FIRE. This I thought he thrust several times through my heart, and that it penetrated my entrails; and as he drew it out again, it seemed to draw them out with it, and to leave me all inflamed with love of God.' The physical experience was so intense that on Teresa's death 23 years later her body was examined and the surrounding nuns claimed her HEART was found pierced with a mark (a relic later claimed to show the wound). Bernini's marble 'Ecstasy of Saint Teresa' (1647-52, Santa Maria della Vittoria, Rome) sculpts this transverberation. T4: pressed by her confessors to write down her experiences for discernment, Teresa produces her LIBRO DE LA VIDA ('Book of Her Life', 1562-65, autobiography), CAMINO DE PERFECCION ('Way of Perfection', 1566, for her nuns), and her masterwork the CASTILLO INTERIOR ('Interior Castle', 1577) — a description of the soul as a crystal castle of SEVEN MANSIONS (moradas) the soul journeys through, each a deeper stage of prayer, culminating in the innermost mansion of union with God. These become foundational texts of Western mysticism. She writes in vigorous Castilian prose, often self-deprecating and funny ('God, deliver me from stupid devotions'), while explaining phenomena no medieval author had described so precisely. T5: her practical work is REFORMING the Carmelite order. In 1562 she founds the first REFORMED (or DISCALCED — 'unshod') Carmelite convent, ST JOSEPH'S in Avila, with strict enclosure, poverty, no servants, and the wearing of coarse habits and rope sandals ('discalced' = shoeless). Over the next twenty years, despite fierce opposition from the 'calced' (unreformed) Carmelites who at one point IMPRISON her collaborator JOHN OF THE CROSS in a Toledo cell for nine months, Teresa founds SEVENTEEN CONVENTS across Spain, traveling in mule-drawn carts over bad roads in extreme heat and cold, negotiating with archbishops, kings (Philip II eventually backed her), and the papal nuncio. She dies at ALBA DE TORMES in 1582, aged 67; her body was later exhumed and reported incorrupt (her heart, hands, and other relics separated across various Carmelite houses). She was canonized 1622 (with Ignatius Loyola, Francis Xavier, Philip Neri, and Isidore the Farmer — the 'five saints' canonization) and named DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH in 1970 by Paul VI — the FIRST WOMAN to receive that title (with Catherine of Siena the same year). Further rungs: her humor — traveling in a cart in a rainstorm she tells God, 'If this is how you treat your friends, no wonder you have so few of them'; her mystical friendship with the poet JOHN OF THE CROSS (next ladder); the calendar-reform coincidence of her death — she died on the night of October 4-15, 1582, the ten days that were dropped when the Gregorian calendar replaced the Julian; the small chapel of the Transverberation preserved at the Incarnation in Avila.

The historical coincidence is real and vivid. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Freya's tears turning to gold when Odur left her, or the Delphic Pythia in her prophetic trance — a woman's mystical experience taken with full seriousness as reported. Teresa's OWN VOICE (funny, self-deprecating, precise) preserved from her writings. The reformed order's founding is honestly practical AND mystical.

name: John of the Cross: the Dark Night of the Soul in the Toledo cell
scope: T1: JUAN DE YEPES Y ALVAREZ is born 1542 at FONTIVEROS in Castile; his father Gonzalo, a converso silk-weaver, dies when he is young; his mother Catalina Alvarez raises three sons on nothing, moving to Medina del Campo where she works as a weaver and John attends a charity school. Small in stature (barely five feet), gentle, brilliant, he enters the CARMELITE order at 21 (1563), takes the name JOHN OF SAINT MATTHIAS, studies at Salamanca (Spain's great university), and is ordained a priest. T2: on the point of leaving the Carmelites for the stricter Carthusians in 1567, he meets in Medina del Campo the fifty-two-year-old Teresa of Avila, who has begun her Carmelite REFORM among women and is looking for men to launch the parallel reform among the friars. She persuades him to stay; on November 28, 1568, John (now called JOHN OF THE CROSS) and two companions found the first reformed men's Carmelite house at a broken-down farmhouse at DURUELO in Castile. T3: in the following years John serves as spiritual director at Teresa's Incarnation convent in Avila (1572-77), guiding the older nun in the deepest phases of her mystical development. But the split between REFORMED (discalced) and UNREFORMED (calced) Carmelites grows bitter; on the night of December 2-3, 1577, calced Carmelite friars raid John's little house in Avila, seize him, and take him under guard to their monastery at TOLEDO where they IMPRISON him in a windowless disused closet six feet by ten, three feet wide at one end, off a friar's cell — the only light coming through a small slit near the ceiling and only during a portion of the day. He is kept there NINE MONTHS. T4: three times a week he is brought to the friars' refectory, fed only bread and water on the floor, and publicly SCOURGED across his shoulders — nine months of this leaves permanent scars visible until his death. His clothing crawls with vermin; the summer heat in Toledo bakes his cell; the winter cold is unbearable; he becomes ill with dysentery. Yet in this cell, in the near-total darkness, he composes his greatest poems in his head — the SPIRITUAL CANTICLE (echoing the Song of Songs), and stanzas that will become the DARK NIGHT OF THE SOUL — writing them down on scraps of paper a kindly new jailer (Juan de Santa Maria) smuggles in during the last weeks. T5: on the night of August 16, 1578, John escapes — loosening the door hinges over weeks, climbing down knotted strips of blanket to a balcony over the Tagus, dropping to a wall, and creeping through the streets in his emaciated state; a nearby Discalced convent shelters him and later evacuates him to Andalusia. Over the next years he expands his prison poems into his four great prose commentaries: ASCENT OF MOUNT CARMEL, DARK NIGHT OF THE SOUL, SPIRITUAL CANTICLE, and LIVING FLAME OF LOVE — the classical texts of Christian mysticism on the soul's ascent, the purgation of the senses and spirit ('the dark night'), and union with God. He continues as prior at various convents (Baeza, Granada, Segovia); in 1591, factional politics among the discalced turn against him too, and he is stripped of office and sent to a remote house at La Penuela and then to Ubeda, where he dies December 14, 1591, aged only 49, from an infected leg abscess. He was canonized 1726 and named DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH in 1926. Further rungs: the two great phrases: 'DARK NIGHT OF THE SOUL' (Dark Night II.6.1) and 'to arrive at what you know not, you must go by a way you know not' (Ascent I.13.11); T.S. Eliot's East Coker III adapting John's paradoxes ('In order to arrive at what you are not / You must go through the way in which you are not'); the modern therapeutic use of 'dark night' has moved far from John's precise meaning (the withdrawal of felt consolation in advanced prayer, not depression); the small height difference between John and Teresa (barely five feet vs. medium height) — Teresa affectionately called him her 'half a friar'.

framing_note: DINNER TEST: T4 — John of the Cross composed his greatest mystical poems (including the SPIRITUAL CANTICLE) IN HIS HEAD, in near-total darkness, in a six-by-ten prison cell where he was flogged three times a week for nine months. The composition-in-prison detail is astonishing and documented. DISTRACTOR MINE: at T1 swap Fontiveros (right) for Avila (Teresa's town — a common mine); at T2 swap Duruelo (first male reformed house, right) for Avila (first female — the mine); at T3 swap the imprisonment city (Toledo right; Salamanca / Segovia / Granada wrong); at T4 swap the cell dimensions (six by ten, three at one end — precisely documented); at T5 swap the escape year (1578); swap Doctor-of-the-Church year (1926) for other real dates. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: T4 stem — 'Held in a windowless cell six feet by ten in Toledo for nine months, flogged three times a week, John composed some of his greatest works — how?' SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell Boethius composing the Consolation of Philosophy in prison awaiting execution — a mind working at its highest in the harshest conditions. HONEST: the persecutors of John were fellow Christian friars, not pagan or non-Christian enemies — the story is about internal Christian factionalism, kept in. His small stature and Teresa's affectionate 'half a friar' nickname humanize him.

name: Francis Xavier: missionary to India and Japan
scope: T1: FRANCISCO DE JASSO Y AZPILICUETA — FRANCIS XAVIER — is born 1506 in the Navarrese castle of XAVIER, seventh of a noble Basque family whose fortunes are destroyed by the Spanish conquest of Navarre in 1512 (Francis's older brothers fought against the Spanish; his father died in exile). Sent to the University of PARIS in 1525 to study, at the College Sainte-Barbe he shares rooms with a fellow Basque, Peter Faber, and later with a much older student — the limping veteran IGNATIUS LOYOLA. T2: Ignatius takes six years to convert Xavier — Xavier resists as a proud young man dreaming of a chivalric career restoring his family — but Ignatius wears him down with a repeated question from the Gospels: 'What shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?' (Mark 8:36). Xavier joins the little band; on August 15, 1534, he is one of the SEVEN COMPANIONS in the crypt at Montmartre taking vows to serve the pope. T3: in 1540, King JOHN III of Portugal asks Pope Paul III for missionaries for his new Asian empire; Ignatius originally names Simao Rodrigues and Nicolas Bobadilla, but Bobadilla falls ill and Ignatius calls Xavier at short notice — Xavier is instructed by Ignatius on the eve of departure, packs in two hours, and sails from Lisbon in April 1541 without ever seeing Ignatius again. After a 13-month voyage he arrives at GOA (Portuguese India) in May 1542. T4: over the next TEN YEARS, Xavier works ceaselessly at the very edge of what any European had done: he preaches along the FISHERY COAST of southern India among the Paravar pearl-divers (baptizing thousands), goes to CEYLON (Sri Lanka), the MOLUCCAS (spice islands), and MALACCA. In 1549, hearing of a distant island empire called JAPAN from a Japanese refugee named ANJIRO whom he had met at Malacca and taught Portuguese, he becomes the FIRST CHRISTIAN MISSIONARY IN JAPAN, landing at KAGOSHIMA on August 15, 1549. He masters Japanese well enough to preach in it (imperfectly), reaches KYOTO in the winter of 1550-51 hoping to convert the emperor (finds a war-shattered city), returns south, and by 1551 has established communities of Japanese Christians (called 'kirishitan') — the FIRST FRUITS of what would grow to c. 300,000 Japanese Christians before the Tokugawa persecutions of the 17th century. T5: still restless, Xavier turns to CHINA — larger, richer, more influential than Japan; if China were converted, Japan and Asia would follow. He returns to Goa briefly (1552), then sails for the Chinese coast; Chinese law forbids foreign entry, so he lands on the small offshore island of SHANGCHUAN (Sancian) near Canton, waiting to bribe a merchant to smuggle him ashore. Struck by fever on the beach in a small hut, unable to reach any European doctor, Xavier dies on December 3, 1552, aged 46, within sight of the Chinese coast he never reached. His body is buried, dug up months later found INCORRUPT (as reported by the Portuguese who came for it), taken to Malacca (also buried and dug up), and finally brought to GOA in 1554 where his body was enshrined in the BASILICA OF BOM JESUS, still visible today (the body has since become mummified and the right arm was removed to Rome in 1615 at Vatican request, where it is on display in the Gesu). He is canonized in 1622 (with Ignatius, Teresa, Philip Neri, Isidore). Pope Pius XI in 1927 declared him CO-PATRON OF ALL MISSIONS with Therese of Lisieux. Further rungs: the estimated 30,000+ people Xavier personally baptized; his letters back to Ignatius (dozens survive, describing conditions in India and Japan in extraordinary detail); his fluency in Japanese as one of the earliest European speakers of the language; the FUJIWARA book of debate summaries with Buddhist monks in Kyoto surviving in Japanese sources; the 1616 Tokugawa Christian ban and the martyr history that follows; the miraculously-preserved right arm shown at the Gesu in Rome; Anjiro (his Japanese informant / co-worker) as the first Japanese Christian.

And the RIGHT ARM removed to Rome in 1615 (still on display at the Gesu church in Rome) while the rest of the body lies in Goa. SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told the way you'd tell a Roman explorer reaching the end of the known world, or Sinbad on his voyages — a real man of remarkable geographical reach and specific known destinations, dates, and endpoint. Honest on the CO-EXISTENCE of Christian missions with Portuguese colonial power (not condemned nor endorsed — presented). The Anjiro story (Japanese informant, first Japanese Christian, named honestly) prevents the mission narrative from being solely European.

name: Erasmus the humanist: 'the prince of the humanists'
scope: T1: DESIDERIUS ERASMUS is born c. 1466 in ROTTERDAM, illegitimate son of a Dutch priest; he attends the school of the BRETHREN OF THE COMMON LIFE at Deventer, orphaned by plague at 13, pushed by guardians into the Augustinian monastery of Steyn where he takes vows (1488) and is ordained priest (1492) but chafes against the enclosed life. He escapes into secretarial and study work outside the monastery and (after 1517) receives papal DISPENSATION from his vows and habit — a rare privilege. T2: over the following decades Erasmus becomes the most famous LIVING scholar in Europe — his Latin swift, elegant, funny; his Greek fluent (rare); his knowledge of the church fathers unmatched. He travels ceaselessly: Paris, Oxford (where he meets Thomas More), Turin (for a doctorate 1506), Bologna, Venice (working with Aldus Manutius at the Aldine Press), Cambridge (professor of Greek), Basel (his printer Johann Froben), Leuven, Freiburg. His CORRESPONDENCE — over 3,000 letters survive — is the greatest single record of the intellectual life of the age. T3: three works make his fame: PRAISE OF FOLLY (Encomium Moriae, 1509 — a title puns on Thomas More's name, written at More's Chelsea house in a week) satirizing the vices of scholars, priests, monks, and popes in the voice of Folly herself; the ADAGIA (1500 and expanded editions) a collection of thousands of ancient Latin and Greek proverbs with commentary — this book taught Europe to speak in the classical idioms it still uses; and his GREEK NEW TESTAMENT (Novum Instrumentum, 1516, printed in Basel) — the FIRST published edition of the New Testament in the original Greek, with his own new Latin translation in parallel. T4: his Greek New Testament is the text Luther works from to make his revolutionary 1522 German translation; Erasmus himself remains inside the Catholic church and refuses to break with Rome. In 1524 he writes DE LIBERO ARBITRIO ('On Free Will') against Luther's determinism; Luther replies harshly with DE SERVO ARBITRIO ('On the Bondage of the Will', 1525) — the exchange marks the definitive break between humanist reform-from-within (Erasmus) and Protestant break-from-without (Luther). Erasmus's saying about this period: 'I LAID THE EGG THAT LUTHER HATCHED' (attributed, probably genuine — with the follow-up 'but the bird I laid was of a very different feather'). T5: Erasmus never marries, never gains a permanent post (refuses cardinalate offers), keeps his intellectual freedom, and dies in BASEL on July 12, 1536, aged about 70. He is buried in the Basel Munster (Protestant by his death, but Erasmus's grave respected). His DYING WORDS reportedly (Beatus Rhenanus): 'LIEVE GOD' — 'DEAR GOD' in his native Dutch, spoken as he slipped from Latin at the last. His libraries and manuscripts are widely dispersed; his editions of the Church Fathers (Jerome, Augustine, Origen, etc.) become the standard scholarly editions for centuries. The Catholic Church places his works on the INDEX OF FORBIDDEN BOOKS in 1559 (the Council of Trent's shadow); the Protestants distrust him for not joining them. Erasmus wanted to be neither Catholic nor Protestant but a Christian humanist who reformed the church from inside through learning — and the split verdict of both sides was itself a kind of vindication of his position. Further rungs: his editions of the church fathers (Jerome, Augustine, Origen, Chrysostom, Cyprian) which stayed the standard scholarly texts for centuries; his COLLOQUIES (dialogues) that taught schoolboys Latin for four hundred years; his friendship with Thomas More; his correspondence with popes and reformers; his refusal to write against Luther for years despite pressure from both sides; his portrait by Hans Holbein the Younger, painted 1523, one of the most famous portraits of the age (in Longford Castle and elsewhere).
